cards.a: Exemplification: Supports a generalization with a series of specific instances. It is best for showing that a pattern is real and widespread rather than isolated.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called comparison-contrast and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Comparison-contrast: Sets two subjects side by side to reveal similarity or difference. It is best for evaluating alternatives; organized point-by-point or subject-by-subject.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called cause-effect and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Cause-effect: Traces why something happened or what it produced. It is best for arguments about responsibility or consequence; must guard against post hoc reasoning.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called process analysis and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Process analysis: Explains the steps by which something happens or is done. It is best for showing feasibility or exposing where a system breaks down.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called classification and division and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Classification and division: Sorts items into categories, or breaks one subject into parts. It is best for imposing order on a sprawling issue so each part can be judged separately.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called problem-solution and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Problem-solution: Establishes a problem, then proposes and defends a remedy. It is best for policy arguments; the solution must be shown to be both effective and feasible.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain why identifying a passage's method of development matters in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The method is itself a rhetorical choice: choosing to define a term, narrate a case, or classify a field shapes what the audience sees as the issue. Naming the method lets you analyze the structure rather than only the sentence-level devices.
cards.n: Analyzing organization is a higher-level move than device-spotting and often supports the sophistication point.

cards.q: Explain what an effective introduction does on an AP Lang essay.
cards.a: It orients the reader to the issue in one or two sentences, narrows to the specific question at stake, and ends with a defensible thesis that previews the line of reasoning. Three to four sentences is plenty.
cards.n: The thesis must appear in the introduction or the conclusion; placing it last in paragraph one is the safest way to secure Row A.

cards.q: Identify introduction moves that waste time or hurt the score.
cards.a: 'Since the beginning of time' openings, dictionary definitions of common words, restating the prompt verbatim, announcing the essay's plan ('In this essay I will'), and long summary of the passage or sources before any claim.
cards.n: Every sentence spent on throat-clearing is a sentence not spent on commentary, which is where 4 of 6 points live.

cards.q: Explain what an effective conclusion does.
cards.a: It extends rather than repeats: it states what follows from the argument, names the stakes or implications, and may broaden to a related context. Two to four sentences is enough.
cards.n: A conclusion is a fine place to earn sophistication by naming limitations or broader implications.

cards.q: Identify conclusion habits to avoid.
cards.a: Mechanically restating the thesis and topic sentences, introducing brand-new evidence that cannot be analyzed, apologizing for the argument, or ending on a rhetorical question that undoes the position just taken.
cards.n: If you are out of time, one strong implication sentence beats a full formulaic restatement.

cards.q: Define the chronological organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Chronological: arranges material in time order. Typical use: narratives, historical causation, and process explanations.

cards.q: Define the spatial organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Spatial: arranges material by physical position or location. Typical use: descriptions of place, scenes, and physical evidence.

cards.q: Define the order of importance organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Order of importance: arranges points from least to most (or most to least) significant. Typical use: persuasion, where ending on the strongest point leaves the final impression.

cards.q: Define the general-to-specific organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: General-to-specific: moves from a broad principle down to particular cases (or the reverse). Typical use: deductive arguments and definitions applied to instances.

cards.q: Explain how to signal an essay's organizational pattern to a reader.
cards.a: Use topic sentences that name the relationship to the previous paragraph, transitions matched to that relationship, and repeated key terms from the thesis, so the pattern is visible without announcing it ('my second point is').

cards.q: Define synthesis as the term is used on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Synthesis is combining material from multiple provided sources with your own reasoning to develop and support your own argument - the sources serve your position, rather than the essay reporting what each source says in turn.
cards.n: The Q1 essay is your argument using sources, not a survey of the sources.

cards.q: Explain how many sources the AP Lang synthesis essay requires and how to use them.
cards.a: You must incorporate and cite at least three of the provided sources in support of your argument; sources may be quoted or paraphrased, and one source can be used in more than one paragraph.
cards.n: Using more than three earns nothing by itself; poor commentary on six sources scores below strong commentary on three.

cards.q: Explain how to cite sources in-text on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Refer to each source by its given label or the author's name in parentheses or in a signal phrase - '(Source C)' or 'Chen argues that...' Full bibliographic citations and a works cited page are not required.
cards.n: Uncited source material can cost the evidence point even if the ideas are accurate.

cards.q: Define an attributive tag (signal phrase) and give two examples.
cards.a: An attributive tag introduces borrowed material and names its origin, so the reader knows where the idea comes from and how to weigh it. Examples: 'As economist Dana Ruiz notes,...' / 'Source B counters that...'
cards.n: Verb choice inside the tag is an argumentative move: 'concedes,' 'claims,' and 'demonstrates' position the source differently.

cards.q: Explain what source-dropping is and how to avoid it.
cards.a: Source-dropping is inserting a quotation or citation with no framing before it and no commentary after it. Avoid it by introducing the source, quoting only the necessary words, and then explaining how it advances your claim.
cards.n: The fix is a sandwich: set up, quote, explain. A paragraph that ends on a quotation almost always needs one more sentence.

cards.q: Explain how to put two sources in conversation rather than listing them.
cards.a: Build the paragraph around your subclaim, then show the relationship between the sources - one extends, complicates, or answers the other - and explain what that relationship proves. The paragraph is organized by idea, not by source.
cards.n: 'While Source A treats cost as decisive, Source D shows the cost falls unevenly' is a conversation; two summaries are not.

cards.q: State the basic MLA in-text citation format for a print source.
cards.a: Author's last name and page number in parentheses with no comma, before the sentence's end punctuation: (Ruiz 42). If the author is named in a signal phrase, only the page number appears: (42).

cards.q: Explain the MLA in-text citation when a source has no page numbers or no named author.
cards.a: With no page numbers (a website), cite the author's name alone. With no author, use a shortened form of the title in quotation marks or italics, matching the works cited entry.

cards.q: Explain how to integrate a quotation grammatically into your own sentence.
cards.a: Make the quotation a syntactic part of your sentence: introduce it with a signal phrase and comma, blend it with 'that' and no comma, or weave short phrases into your own clause. The finished sentence must parse if the quotation marks were removed.
cards.n: Read the sentence aloud without the quotation marks - if it is ungrammatical, the integration failed.

cards.q: Explain when and how to use an ellipsis in a quotation.
cards.a: Use three spaced periods ( ... ) to mark words omitted from the middle of a quotation, and only when the omission does not change the author's meaning. No ellipsis is needed at the start of a quoted fragment.
cards.n: Cutting a qualifier out of a quotation with an ellipsis is a form of cherry picking, not a mechanical fix.

cards.q: Explain when to use square brackets inside a quotation.
cards.a: Use square brackets to insert your own words for clarity or grammatical fit - identifying a pronoun's referent, adjusting a verb tense, or changing capitalization - so the quotation reads correctly in your sentence.
cards.n: Brackets signal editing by you; anything inside them is your language, not the source's.

cards.q: Explain the 'so what' link that ends a body paragraph.
cards.a: The final sentence should state why the paragraph's subclaim matters to the thesis - the consequence, stake, or step it establishes - rather than restating the topic sentence in different words.
cards.n: This one sentence per paragraph is the cheapest reliable way to raise a Row B score.

cards.q: Explain where to place the counterargument paragraph and why.
cards.a: Place it after your strongest supporting paragraphs and before the conclusion, so the reader is already persuaded when the objection appears and you have the last word answering it. State the objection fairly, then refute or absorb it.
cards.n: Handling a genuine counterargument with nuance is one recognized route to the sophistication point.

cards.q: State the overall format of the AP English Language and Composition exam.
cards.a: Section I: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, worth 45% of the score. Section II: three free-response essays in 2 hours 15 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period), worth 55%.
cards.h: → two sections with times and weights
cards.n: Total testing time is 3 hours 15 minutes; the FRQs are worth more than the entire MC section.

cards.q: State what Section I of the AP Lang exam contains.
cards.a: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes across five or so passages, split between reading questions (rhetorical analysis of nonfiction passages) and writing questions (revising a draft passage for argument, evidence, and style).
cards.n: Roughly 23-25 reading-analysis questions and 20-22 writing/revision questions - budget about 80 seconds per question.

cards.q: Contrast the two kinds of multiple-choice questions on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Reading questions ask what a published passage does - the writer's choices, purpose, audience, and reasoning. Writing questions present a student draft and ask which revision best achieves a stated goal, such as adding evidence or improving a transition.
cards.n: Writing questions always name a goal; the right answer is the one that serves that goal, not the prettiest sentence.

cards.q: State the structure of Section II of the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Three essays in 2 hours 15 minutes: Q1 Synthesis, Q2 Rhetorical Analysis, Q3 Argument. The first 15 minutes are a suggested reading period for the synthesis source packet; each essay is then given about 40 minutes.
cards.n: The essays are equally weighted, so never let one essay eat another's time.

cards.q: Explain how to use the 15-minute reading period.
cards.a: Read the Q1 prompt first, decide a tentative position, then skim all sources marking each one's stance and one usable quotation. Sketch a three-part line of reasoning. You may begin writing before the 15 minutes end.
cards.n: Reading sources without a position first is the main way students burn the reading period.

cards.q: Identify what the synthesis question (Q1) demands.
cards.a: Take a defensible position on the issue and develop an argument that incorporates and cites at least three of six or seven provided sources as support. The sources are evidence for your claim, not the subject of the essay.
cards.n: The prompt's phrasing is usually 'develop a position' - a summary of the debate with no position cannot earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the rhetorical analysis question (Q2) demands.
cards.a: Read a nonfiction passage with a given rhetorical situation, then analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes to achieve their purpose - explaining how and why the choices work on that audience, not merely which devices appear.
cards.n: The thesis must name the writer's message or purpose; a list of devices alone does not earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the argument question (Q3) demands.
cards.a: Respond to a short prompt or quotation by taking your own defensible position and supporting it with evidence you supply - personal experience, observation, reading, history, current events - developed with commentary.
cards.n: No passage is provided, so evidence quality is entirely on you; specific named examples beat general assertions.

cards.q: State the three rows of the AP Lang essay rubric and their point values.
cards.a: Row A: Thesis, 0-1 point. Row B: Evidence and Commentary, 0-4 points. Row C: Sophistication, 0-1 point. Total 6 points per essay.
cards.n: The same 6-point rubric applies to all three essays; Row B alone is two-thirds of the score.

cards.q: Explain exactly what earns the Row A thesis point.
cards.a: One point for a defensible thesis that responds to the prompt with a position, and that may preview the line of reasoning. It must be in the introduction or conclusion and be more than a restatement of the prompt.
cards.n: It is all-or-nothing: a partially defensible thesis earns zero, not a half point.

cards.q: Identify the most common reasons students lose the Row A point.
cards.a: Restating the prompt; describing the passage or sources instead of claiming; listing devices with no message ('the author uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); an obvious, undebatable statement; or a thesis buried mid-essay with nothing in the intro or conclusion.
cards.n: Write the thesis last in paragraph one, in one sentence, and make sure a reasonable person could disagree with it.

cards.q: Explain the Row B scale from 0 to 4.
cards.a: 0: no relevant evidence, or the response only restates the thesis. 1: mostly general evidence, and/or evidence summarized rather than explained. 2: some specific relevant evidence, with explanation of how some of it relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or the line of reasoning is faulty. 3: specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning, with explanation of how some of the evidence supports that line of reasoning. 4: specific evidence for all claims in a line of reasoning, with commentary that consistently explains how the evidence supports it.
cards.n: The jump from 1 to 2 is the jump from summarizing evidence to explaining it; the jump from 2 to 3 is establishing a real line of reasoning.

cards.q: Contrast a Row B score of 3 and a Row B score of 4.
cards.a: A 3 supports most claims with specific evidence and explains some of it. A 4 sustains it: every claim has specific, well-chosen evidence and the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports a coherent line of reasoning.
cards.n: Consistency and a visible line of reasoning are the difference; one brilliant paragraph among three thin ones is a 3.

cards.q: Explain what the Row C sophistication point rewards.
cards.a: One point for a response that demonstrates sophistication of thought or a complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, sustained across the essay rather than shown in a single sentence.
cards.n: Fewer than one in ten essays earns this point; it cannot be faked with grand-sounding closing lines.

cards.q: Identify the recognized routes to earning the sophistication point.
cards.a: Explaining the significance or implications of the argument in a broader context; explaining the tensions, contradictions, or nuances within the issue; consistently engaging the complexity of the rhetorical situation; or writing with a vivid, persuasive style that is consistently controlled.
cards.n: Choose one route and sustain it; attempting all four superficially reads as unfocused.

cards.q: Identify what does NOT earn the sophistication point.
cards.a: Sweeping generalizations ('humans have always struggled with this'), a single fancy sentence, unsupported claims about society, dense vocabulary without substance, and hedged both-sides commentary that never commits.
cards.n: Readers are told to reward sustained complexity, not isolated flourishes.

cards.q: State a workable timing plan for the AP Lang free-response section.
cards.a: 15 minutes reading and planning Q1; 40 minutes writing Q1; 5 minutes planning and 35 minutes writing Q2; 5 minutes planning and 30 minutes writing Q3; 5 minutes final check. Wear a watch and switch essays on schedule even if unfinished.
cards.n: Three complete decent essays outscore two excellent ones plus a fragment, because each is scored independently out of 6.

cards.q: Explain how to read a synthesis source set quickly.
cards.a: Read the prompt and take a position first. Then, for each source, read the header, the first and last paragraph, and skim the middle, jotting a two-word stance label and starring one usable line. Note which sources conflict - that tension is where sophistication lives.
cards.n: Charts and images count as sources and are underused; they often supply the cleanest data point.

cards.q: Explain how to write a rhetorical analysis body paragraph.
cards.a: Name the rhetorical choice; quote the specific evidence briefly; explain the effect on the intended audience; then link that effect to the writer's overall purpose. Choice, evidence, effect, purpose - in that order, every paragraph.
cards.n: The 'effect' and 'purpose' steps are the ones students skip, and they are exactly where Row B points live.

cards.q: Explain how to organize a rhetorical analysis essay other than device by device.
cards.a: Organize by the argument's movement: how the writer shifts from establishing credibility, to intensifying urgency, to demanding action - analyzing choices as they serve each stage. This foregrounds purpose instead of cataloguing techniques.
cards.n: Chunking the passage by rhetorical purpose is the surest structural route away from device-hunting.

cards.q: Identify why 'device-hunting' lowers a rhetorical analysis score.
cards.a: Naming devices without explaining their effect produces evidence with no commentary, capping Row B at 1 or 2. A correct label ('this is anaphora') proves nothing about how the passage works on its audience.
cards.n: You may earn a 6 without naming a single device by name, as long as you explain the choices.

cards.q: Identify why summarizing the passage or sources lowers a score.
cards.a: Summary reports content; the rubric rewards analysis of how content works. A summary-driven essay usually has no defensible thesis (Row A zero) and evidence without commentary (Row B 1-2).
cards.n: If your paragraph could be written by someone who agreed with nothing you believe, it is summary.

cards.q: Explain why five-paragraph autopilot hurts on AP Lang.
cards.a: The formula forces exactly three body paragraphs whether the argument needs two or five, encourages one-source-per-paragraph listing, and spends space on formulaic intros and restating conclusions instead of commentary. Let the line of reasoning set the paragraph count.
cards.n: There is no required number of paragraphs; readers score reasoning, not shape.

cards.q: Explain how to handle the argument essay's requirement to take a position.
cards.a: State one clear position in the thesis and hold it. You may qualify - agree with limits or under conditions - but you must be committed enough that a reader could argue against you; balanced 'both sides have points' essays fail Row A.
cards.n: Qualifying is not fence-sitting: 'X is justified only when Y' is a strong, defensible position.

cards.q: Define what an AP prompt means by 'evaluate.'
cards.a: To evaluate is to judge the merit, validity, or effectiveness of something against criteria and to argue for that judgment - not to describe or summarize it.

cards.q: Explain the 'defend, challenge, or qualify' instruction on an AP Lang prompt.
cards.a: Defend means argue the claim is right; challenge means argue it is wrong; qualify means agree in part while specifying the conditions or limits under which it holds. You must choose one and sustain it - all three are equally scoreable.
cards.n: Qualify is usually the most defensible choice because it lets you use counterevidence as support.

cards.q: Explain how to write a strong qualified position.
cards.a: Name what you accept in the claim, name the conditions or cases where it fails, and state the principle that separates them. 'Civil disobedience is justified when legal channels have been exhausted, but not when the cause has not yet been argued publicly.'
cards.n: A qualified thesis must still be one sentence with one governing position, not two claims joined by 'but.'

cards.q: Explain how to use the context paragraph that precedes an FRQ passage.
cards.a: It supplies the rhetorical situation - writer, audience, occasion, exigence, and purpose - which the analysis must use. Mining it for audience and occasion is the fastest way to make commentary specific rather than generic.
cards.h: → what it gives + how to use
cards.n: Ignoring the framing paragraph is a common cause of vague, audience-free commentary on Q2.

cards.q: Explain what a Q2 rhetorical analysis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state the writer's purpose or message and indicate the kinds of choices used to achieve it, in a way that can be developed - not a list of devices and not a summary of the passage's topic.
cards.n: 'Uses ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade the audience' is the classic Row A zero.

cards.q: Explain what a Q1 synthesis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state your own defensible position on the prompt's issue, specific enough to be argued with the sources, and it should suggest the reasoning that will organize the essay. It should not simply report what the sources collectively say.

cards.q: Explain what counts as acceptable evidence on the Q3 argument essay.
cards.a: Anything specific and accurate: history, current events, literature, film, science, personal experience, or observation. Readers do not privilege one domain; they reward specificity, accuracy, and the commentary that connects it to the claim.
cards.n: Two developed examples with real commentary beat five name-dropped ones.

cards.q: Explain the ratio of evidence to commentary you should aim for.
cards.a: Roughly one sentence of evidence to two of commentary. If a paragraph is mostly quotation or mostly source summary, it is under-analyzed no matter how apt the evidence is.
cards.n: Highlight your quotations: if more than a third of a body paragraph is highlighted, cut evidence and add commentary.

cards.q: State a 5-minute end-of-essay checklist.
cards.a: Does the thesis take a defensible position? Does each topic sentence make a claim? Is every quotation followed by explanation? Are at least three sources cited (Q1)? Does the last sentence of each paragraph tie back to the thesis?

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice reading questions.
cards.a: Read the question stem before rereading the lines, return to the cited lines and their surrounding context, predict an answer in your own words, then find the choice closest to it. Eliminate choices that are true of the passage but do not answer the stem.
cards.n: The most common wrong answer is accurate about the passage but irrelevant to what the question asked.

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice writing/revision questions.
cards.a: Identify the stated goal in the stem (add evidence, sharpen the claim, improve the transition), then judge each option only against that goal. Read the sentences before and after the insertion point, since the answer usually depends on that link.
cards.n: Grammatically fine but goal-irrelevant options are the standard distractors here.

cards.q: State the guessing policy and pacing target for the multiple-choice section.
cards.a: There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. With 45 questions in 60 minutes, the pace is about 80 seconds per question, or roughly 11-12 minutes per passage set.
cards.n: Never leave a blank; mark and return rather than stalling on one hard question.

cards.q: Explain how to annotate a passage efficiently during the exam.
cards.a: The exam is fully digital in Bluebook, so annotate with the app's highlight and note tools rather than a pen: highlight the shifts (but, yet, however), the audience and occasion clues, and one or two places where tone changes, and drop a short note where each purpose-driven chunk of the passage begins. Do not highlight every device you recognize.
cards.h: → what to mark + what to skip
cards.n: Annotation should produce a structure you can write from, not a decorated page.

cards.q: State how AP Lang exam scores are reported and composed.
cards.a: The final AP score is a 1-5 scale. It combines the multiple-choice section (45%) with the three free-response essays (55%), each essay scored 0-6 on the same rubric and weighted equally.
cards.n: A composite around half the available points typically reaches a 3; exact cut scores shift each year.

cards.q: Explain how AP readers score the essays.
cards.a: Each essay is scored row by row against the 6-point analytic rubric by a trained reader, independently of your other essays, and readers are instructed to reward what the response does well rather than deduct for what is missing.
cards.n: There is no penalty carried across essays: a weak Q1 does not lower your Q2 score.

cards.q: Explain how grammar and mechanics affect an AP Lang essay score.
cards.a: There is no separate grammar row. Errors matter only when they interfere with the reader's understanding of the argument; a well-reasoned essay with imperfect surface polish can still earn 6.
cards.n: This is not license to ignore clarity - unreadable sentences do cost points through Row B.

cards.q: Explain what happens if an essay does not respond to the prompt.
cards.a: Responses that are off-topic, that only repeat the prompt, or that are written in a language other than English receive a score of 0. A blank or completely blank-page response receives no score at all.

cards.q: Decide what to do when you have 10 minutes left and no essay started on Q3.
cards.a: Write a one-sentence defensible thesis immediately, then two body paragraphs with one specific example each and two sentences of commentary each. Skip the introduction beyond the thesis and skip the conclusion. Thesis plus real commentary can still earn 3-4 points.
cards.n: A thesis with two developed paragraphs scores far above a polished intro with nothing after it.

cards.q: Explain how to plan an essay in five minutes.
cards.a: Write the thesis in one sentence, then list two to four subclaims in the order they build, and note the single piece of evidence attached to each. That list is your topic sentences; if the subclaims do not build, reorder before writing.

cards.q: Identify habits that make commentary generic.
cards.a: Naming the audience as 'the reader' rather than the specific audience; explaining that a choice makes the argument 'more effective' or 'more persuasive' without saying how; and repeating the thesis instead of advancing it.
cards.n: Replace 'this is effective' with 'this makes a skeptical legislator feel the cost personally.'

cards.q: Define monosyllabic diction and give an example.
cards.a: Word choice built mainly from one-syllable words, which reads as plain, blunt, or direct. e.g. We must act now, or we lose all we have built.
cards.n: Effect: strips away ornament so the claim lands with the force of plain speech.

cards.q: Define polysyllabic diction and give an example.
cards.a: Word choice built from words of many syllables, which reads as elevated, formal, or intellectual. e.g. the unprecedented deterioration of institutional accountability.
cards.n: Effect: signals expertise and gravity but risks sounding evasive to a general audience.

cards.q: Contrast Latinate and Anglo-Saxon diction.
cards.a: Anglo-Saxon diction uses short, native English words and sounds plain and direct; Latinate diction uses longer words borrowed from Latin or French and sounds formal or bureaucratic. Home versus residence is the classic pair.
cards.n: Writers often switch registers mid-passage; the switch itself is worth analyzing.

cards.q: Define loaded diction and give an example.
cards.a: Word choice selected specifically for its strong emotional connotation, used to sway judgment rather than merely describe. e.g. calling a proposal a scheme rather than a plan.

cards.q: Define plain style and give an example.
cards.a: A style using simple, direct, largely concrete diction and short sentences, avoiding ornamentation. e.g. Hemingway's declarative prose: The old man was thin and gaunt.

cards.q: Contrast ethos and credibility.
cards.a: Ethos is the rhetorical appeal that draws on a speaker's character; credibility is the specific quality of trustworthiness the audience must grant before that appeal works. A speaker can attempt ethos and still fail to earn credibility.
cards.n: Credibility is earned moment to moment in the text; ethos is the category of appeal it belongs to.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates: 'Picture the empty chair at every table this disease has left behind.'
cards.a: Pathos. The imagined image of loss is designed to produce grief and urgency rather than to supply data or credentials.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates: 'The CDC's own data show infection rates fell 40 percent after the mandate.'
cards.a: Logos, with a supporting layer of ethos from the cited authority. The statistic is offered as evidence a skeptical reader can verify, not as an emotional image.

cards.q: Explain why an appeal can backfire with a particular audience.
cards.a: An appeal backfires when it assumes values, knowledge, or trust the audience does not actually hold: heavy pathos can read as manipulative to a skeptical audience, and technical logos can alienate a general one.
cards.n: Judging fit to audience, not just naming the appeal, is what separates analysis from labeling.

cards.q: Identify the move: 'Cutting the budget will save money short term - but it guts the programs that prevent costlier crises later.'
cards.a: Concession followed by refutation. The writer grants the opponent's short-term point before pivoting on but to reassert the original position.

cards.q: Identify the move: 'Some will say this policy asks too much of small towns. It asks exactly what fairness requires of everyone.'
cards.a: Counterargument followed by rebuttal. The writer states the objection directly, then answers it rather than ignoring it.

cards.q: Define a straw man rebuttal and explain why it damages ethos even when it wins the exchange.
cards.a: A straw man rebuttal answers a weakened, distorted version of the opponent's actual claim. It can look like a win in the moment, but an alert audience notices the substitution and distrusts the writer's fairness afterward.
cards.n: The logical version of this move is defined under fallacies; here the angle is audience trust, not validity.

cards.q: Define a hostile audience and the adjustment it typically demands.
cards.a: An audience predisposed to reject the writer's claim. It typically demands more concession, a calmer tone, and common ground established early, rather than a direct opening assertion.

cards.q: Define the universal audience as a rhetorical concept.
cards.a: An imagined audience of all reasonable people, used as a standard: an argument aimed at it relies on reasoning any rational person would accept, not on the particular biases of one group.
cards.n: Useful for judging whether an appeal is genuinely persuasive or only plays to one faction's assumptions.

cards.q: Contrast a sympathetic and an undecided audience in terms of what a writer must do.
cards.a: A sympathetic audience already agrees and mainly needs energy or language to act; an undecided audience needs to be informed and moved from neutrality, so the writer must build the case from shared premises rather than assume agreement.

cards.q: Contrast constraints and resources within the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: Constraints are limits that restrict a writer's choices, such as time, length, or a hostile audience; resources are advantages a writer can draw on, such as shared history or existing credibility. The same fact can function as either.

cards.q: Define genre as it functions within the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The recognized category or form a text belongs to (eulogy, op-ed, open letter, commencement address), which sets audience expectations about length, tone, and structure before a word is read.
cards.n: A writer who breaks genre conventions is making a choice worth analyzing, not making an error.

cards.q: Apply SOAPSTone: explain why it has no separate letter for exigence.
cards.a: SOAPSTone has no slot for exigence; Occasion covers the surface event, so the prompting urgency has to be inferred from Occasion and Subject together rather than read off a single letter.

cards.q: Contrast tone and diction as objects of analysis.
cards.a: Diction is the raw material, the specific words chosen; tone is the attitude those words add up to. You name tone with an adjective and prove it by pointing to the diction that produces it.

cards.q: Identify the tone shift: 'The garden had been his pride for forty years. Now the county wants to pave it for a parking lot.'
cards.a: A shift from a warm, nostalgic tone to a bitter or indignant one, marked by the pivot word now and the change from loving description to blunt fact.

cards.q: Define an elegiac tone and give an example occasion.
cards.a: A mournful, reflective tone appropriate to loss or death, often blending grief with tribute. e.g. a eulogy that dwells on what a community has lost alongside what the person gave it.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inform.
cards.a: To convey facts or explain a subject clearly to an audience without primarily arguing a contested position, though the selection of facts can still carry a slant worth noticing.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to console.
cards.a: To offer comfort to an audience experiencing grief or hardship, typically by affirming shared feeling, meaning, or hope rather than by arguing a claim.

cards.q: Contrast a text's stated purpose and its functional purpose.
cards.a: The stated purpose is what a text claims to be doing, such as informing; the functional purpose is what its choices actually accomplish, such as persuading through selective facts. Analysis should test one against the other.
cards.n: A text that claims neutrality while loading its diction is a classic AP Lang analysis target.

cards.q: State the five classical canons of rhetoric.
cards.a: Invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery - the five arts ancient rhetoricians used to compose and deliver a speech, from finding arguments to the final performance.
cards.n: AP Lang draws heavily on arrangement and style; invention maps onto claims and evidence.

cards.q: Define invention as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The process of discovering and developing the arguments, evidence, and lines of reasoning available for a given issue and audience - generating what to say before deciding how to say it.

cards.q: Define delivery as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The manner in which a speech is physically performed - voice, gesture, pacing, presence - as opposed to the words themselves; in written rhetoric it maps loosely onto formatting and tone of presentation.

cards.q: Contrast a valid argument and a sound argument.
cards.a: An argument is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its premises, regardless of whether the premises are true. It is sound only if it is valid AND all its premises are actually true.
cards.n: A perfectly valid syllogism built on a false premise proves nothing about reality - a classic MC trap.

cards.q: Identify the type of reasoning: 'Every cygnet observed this spring on the lake was white, so the town's swans are a white species.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning. It moves from a set of specific observed instances to a general, merely probable conclusion about the whole category.

cards.q: Identify the type of reasoning: 'All municipal bonds are tax-exempt. This is a municipal bond. Therefore this bond is tax-exempt.'
cards.a: Deductive reasoning. It moves from a general premise through a specific case to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true.

cards.q: Contrast a primary and a secondary source.
cards.a: A primary source is firsthand: original data, a speech transcript, an eyewitness account, a raw document. A secondary source analyzes or reports on primary material, such as a journalist's summary of a study.
cards.n: On the synthesis essay, naming a source as primary or secondary can support a claim about its reliability.

cards.q: Define a spurious (false) correlation and give an example.
cards.a: A statistical association between two variables with no real causal connection, often produced by coincidence or a hidden third factor. e.g. ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer because of heat, not each other.
cards.n: This is the statistical version of post hoc reasoning - correlation mistaken for causation.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'Requiring a civics course should not be optional for graduation.'
cards.a: A claim of policy. It uses should and urges a specific action, rather than asserting a fact or judging worth in the abstract.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'A four-day school week is worse for working families than a traditional schedule.'
cards.a: A claim of value. It judges the schedule as worse against an implied standard (impact on working families) rather than asserting a checkable fact or urging an action.

cards.q: Define burden of proof in argumentation.
cards.a: The obligation to provide sufficient evidence and reasoning for a claim before an audience is required to accept it. The burden rests on whoever makes the claim, especially one that departs from the status quo.
cards.n: A policy claim proposing change carries a heavier burden of proof than one defending current practice.

cards.q: Define data (grounds) in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Data, or grounds, is the specific evidence or facts offered as the foundation for a claim - the concrete support the warrant then links to that claim.
cards.n: Grounds is the Toulmin term for what the rest of the deck calls evidence.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Senator Cole wants stricter emissions limits, but why listen to someone who just bought a second house?'
cards.a: Ad hominem. It attacks Senator Cole's personal choices instead of addressing the merits of the emissions proposal.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'She wants schools to teach media literacy, which just means she thinks students are too dumb to think for themselves.'
cards.a: Straw man. It replaces the actual proposal with an exaggerated, easier-to-attack version and refutes that instead.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Either we privatize the water utility, or the whole system collapses within a year.'
cards.a: False dilemma. It presents only two extreme outcomes when other options, such as partial reform or new funding, are available.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'If we let students redo one quiz, soon every assignment will be optional and no one will learn anything.'
cards.a: Slippery slope. It claims one small allowance will inevitably cascade into total collapse without showing why each step must follow.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'I met two rude tourists from that city, so people from there must all be unfriendly.'
cards.a: Hasty generalization. It draws a sweeping conclusion about an entire population from a sample of two encounters.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'The team started winning right after they changed the mascot, so the new mascot must be the reason.'
cards.a: Post hoc ergo propter hoc. It assumes the earlier event caused the later one merely because it came first.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This painting is a masterpiece because a true genius made it, and we know she's a genius because look at this masterpiece.'
cards.a: Circular reasoning (begging the question). The conclusion is used to prove the premise, which is then used to prove the conclusion again.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This diet must work - a famous actor swears by it in every interview.'
cards.a: Appeal to authority (fallacious). The actor's fame, not any relevant nutritional expertise, is offered as proof the diet works.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Everyone at school already has the new phone, so obviously you need one too.'
cards.a: Bandwagon (appeal to popularity). It treats widespread adoption as proof that owning the phone is necessary or correct.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Why worry about the factory's emissions when there's so much litter downtown nobody cleans up?'
cards.a: Red herring. It diverts attention from the emissions question to an unrelated issue instead of addressing the original point.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'You say I text too much at dinner, but you're always checking email at the table too.'
cards.a: Tu quoque. It deflects the criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior instead of answering whether it is valid.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'A light diet is better for you, and light things are easier to lift, so a light diet makes you stronger.'
cards.a: Equivocation. The word light shifts meaning midargument from low in calories to low in weight, so the reasoning only appears to connect.

cards.q: Define apophasis and give an example.
cards.a: Bringing up a subject by claiming to pass over it, so the audience registers the point while the speaker denies making it. e.g. I won't mention his three arrests, since that has nothing to do with tonight's vote.
cards.n: Effect: delivers the accusation while preserving deniability, so the speaker seems fair while still landing the blow.

cards.q: Define procatalepsis and give an example.
cards.a: Anticipating an opponent's objection and answering it before the opponent can raise it. e.g. Some will say this plan costs too much - but doing nothing will cost far more within a decade.
cards.n: Effect: seizes control of the argument's agenda and makes the speaker look prepared rather than defensive.

cards.q: Contrast procatalepsis and hypophora.
cards.a: Procatalepsis raises and answers an opponent's objection to defuse it in advance; hypophora raises the writer's own question and answers it to structure an argument. One preempts a challenge, the other organizes an explanation.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The senator lost her temper and, moments later, the vote.'
cards.a: Zeugma. The single verb lost governs two different objects, temper and the vote, in two different senses at once.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We will rebuild after the flood. We will rebuild after the fire. We will rebuild after every disaster.'
cards.a: Anaphora. The phrase We will rebuild repeats at the start of each successive clause, building momentum toward the final claim.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'This is a plan built by workers, tested by workers, and paid for by workers.'
cards.a: Epistrophe. The phrase by workers repeats at the end of each successive clause, so the audience leaves the sentence holding that phrase.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The company promised safety for its workers and profit for its owners; it delivered profit for its owners and injury for its workers.'
cards.a: Chiasmus. The grammatical structure of the first clause reverses in the second (ABBA), though the words are not all repeated.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The company did not choose its workers; the workers chose the company.'
cards.a: Antimetabole. The same words (company, workers, choose) repeat in reversed grammatical order, making the reversal itself the point.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The council voted, the funding passed, the project began.'
cards.a: Asyndeton. The conjunctions between the three clauses are omitted, giving the sequence a rapid, almost breathless pace.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'And the delays and the excuses and the broken promises finally caught up with the campaign.'
cards.a: Polysyndeton. The conjunction and repeats before every item, slowing the sentence and making the accumulation feel heavy and relentless.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The proposal is not without its problems.'
cards.a: Litotes. The claim is affirmed by negating its opposite (not without problems), which softens the criticism into understatement.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The plan requires patience. Patience is what the board has never had.'
cards.a: Anadiplosis. The last word of the first sentence, patience, becomes the first substantive word of the next, chaining the two ideas together.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'I hardly know how to answer such an accusation - where would a person even begin?'
cards.a: Aporia. The speaker expresses genuine or feigned uncertainty about how to respond, which can disarm the audience before a confident reply follows.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'What do we owe the next generation? We owe them a planet no worse than the one we inherited.'
cards.a: Hypophora. The writer poses a question and then immediately supplies the answer, controlling the direction of the argument.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The old factory brought jobs to this town; the new one brought only debt.'
cards.a: Antithesis. Two contrasting ideas, jobs and debt, are set against each other in parallel grammatical structure to sharpen the comparison.

cards.q: Identify the device: a report describes the CEO's newly renovated yacht in one paragraph and the factory's broken safety gear in the next.
cards.a: Juxtaposition. Placing the two contrasting images side by side, without commentary, lets the reader draw the unflattering comparison unaided.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Every reform since has been measured against that summer, the district's own Waterloo.'
cards.a: Allusion. The brief, unexplained reference to Waterloo borrows the shared cultural meaning of a final, crushing defeat without spelling it out.

cards.q: Identify the device: after a factory explosion injures dozens, an executive calls it 'a bit of an inconvenience for the schedule.'
cards.a: Understatement. Describing a serious, injury-causing event as a minor inconvenience deliberately minimizes it; the gap reads as callous or evasive.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'After the vote failed, after the funding dried up, after the last volunteer quit, the clinic finally closed.'
cards.a: Periodic sentence. The main clause, the clinic finally closed, is withheld until the end, after introductory clauses build suspense toward it.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'The clinic closed, its doors locked, its equipment sold, its patients scattered to clinics an hour away.'
cards.a: Loose (cumulative) sentence. The main clause, the clinic closed, comes first, and modifying details pile on afterward to enrich it.

cards.q: Identify the voice and its likely rhetorical purpose: 'Mistakes were made in the handling of the funds.'
cards.a: Passive voice. The sentence omits who made the mistakes, letting the writer avoid naming or blaming a specific actor - a common evasive use of passive construction.
cards.n: Contrast with active: The treasurer misused the funds names the actor directly.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'How much longer can this city pretend the water is safe to drink?'
cards.a: Rhetorical question. It is posed not to gather an answer but to imply one, drawing the audience into agreeing without stating the claim outright.

cards.q: Contrast metaphor and simile.
cards.a: A simile compares two unlike things explicitly using like or as; a metaphor asserts that one thing is the other with no comparing word. Metaphor states the equation outright, while simile keeps it at arm's length.
cards.n: Simile is easier to defend as illustrative; metaphor commits harder and so carries more persuasive risk and force.

cards.q: Contrast euphony and cacophony.
cards.a: Euphony arranges sounds to be pleasing and harmonious, typically soft consonants and long vowels; cacophony arranges sounds to be harsh and discordant, typically hard consonants in clusters. The sound signals the writer's judgment.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal comparison and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Comparison: similarly, likewise, in the same way, by the same token. They signal to the reader that what follows is alike in kind to what came before.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal condition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Condition: if, unless, provided that, as long as, in the event that. They signal to the reader that what follows depends on a stated circumstance rather than holding unconditionally.

cards.q: Define pronoun reference as a coherence device and its main risk.
cards.a: Using pronouns (it, this, they) to point back to a previously named idea, linking sentences without repeating the noun. Its main risk is an unclear antecedent, which leaves the reader guessing what it refers to.

cards.q: Define key-term repetition as a coherence device.
cards.a: Deliberately repeating a thesis's central word or phrase across topic sentences and transitions so the reader keeps tracking the same idea as it develops.
cards.n: Repeating the exact term from the prompt or thesis is a cheap, reliable way to keep an essay visibly unified.

cards.q: Contrast narration and description as methods of development.
cards.a: Narration tells a sequence of events as a story, organized in time; description renders sensory, concrete detail about a subject or scene, organized in space or impression. Narration moves; description dwells.

cards.q: Contrast classification and division as methods of development.
cards.a: Classification sorts many separate items into shared categories; division breaks one single subject into its component parts. Classification groups outward from many things; division splits inward from one thing.

cards.q: Define the categorical (topical) organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Categorical: arranges material by distinct types or categories rather than by time, space, or importance. Typical use: essays that survey several kinds of causes, groups, or examples side by side.

cards.q: Contrast point-by-point and block organization for a comparison-contrast essay.
cards.a: Point-by-point alternates between the two subjects within each paragraph, comparing one criterion at a time; block covers all of one subject first, then all of the other. Point-by-point keeps the comparison constant; block risks two disconnected halves.
cards.n: Point-by-point is usually safer under exam time pressure because the comparison stays visible throughout.

cards.q: Contrast paraphrase and direct quotation as ways to use a source.
cards.a: Paraphrase restates a source's idea in your own words, useful for background or dense material; direct quotation preserves exact wording, useful when the phrasing itself is evidence, such as loaded diction or a striking claim.
cards.n: Overusing direct quotation when paraphrase would serve better is a common way essays drift into summary.

cards.q: Define a block quotation and its MLA formatting trigger.
cards.a: A quotation of more than four lines of prose, set off from the paragraph as an indented block without quotation marks, with the parenthetical citation placed after the final punctuation.
cards.n: On a timed AP Lang essay, block quotations rarely earn their space; short, closely analyzed quotations score better.

cards.q: Explain the scoring consequence of citing fewer than three sources on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: The response cannot earn full Row B credit, since the task requires evidence drawn from and cited to at least three sources; reasoning built on personal opinion alone, however well developed, is scored as under-evidenced.

cards.q: Contrast unity and coherence in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence supports the one idea in the topic sentence, with nothing off-topic; coherence means the sentences connect smoothly through transitions and reference, so the idea's development is easy to follow.
cards.n: A paragraph can be unified but still incoherent if its on-topic sentences jump around without links.

cards.q: Identify four effective ways to open an AP Lang essay besides stating the thesis outright.
cards.a: A brief relevant anecdote, a striking statistic, a short apt quotation, or a specific concrete scenario tied directly to the issue. Each should lead in one or two sentences to the thesis, not wander.

cards.q: Explain the call-to-action technique as a way to end an argument essay.
cards.a: The conclusion names a specific action the audience should take or a specific change that should follow from the argument, converting the essay's claim into a concrete next step rather than a restated summary.

cards.q: Explain the difference between macro transitions and micro transitions.
cards.a: Macro transitions connect one paragraph to the next, signaling how the whole subclaim relates to the last; micro transitions connect sentences within a single paragraph, guiding the reader through one line of thought.

cards.q: Explain why a chart, photograph, or cartoon in a synthesis source set counts as a citable source.
cards.a: The prompt treats every numbered source as eligible evidence regardless of format; a graphic makes an argument through its data or imagery just as a prose source does, and citing it satisfies the three-source requirement.

cards.q: Explain what it means for a thesis to preview (roadmap) the line of reasoning.
cards.a: The thesis briefly signals the order or categories of support to come, such as naming the grounds the essay will argue from, so the reader knows the shape of the argument before the body paragraphs begin.
cards.n: A roadmap thesis is not required for the Row A point, but it makes the reasoning easier for a reader to follow.

cards.q: Define plagiarism as it applies to the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Presenting a source's words or ideas as your own without attribution, whether by omitting a citation or by paraphrasing too closely to the original wording without crediting the source.

cards.q: Contrast a coordinating conjunction and a conjunctive adverb as transitional tools.
cards.a: A coordinating conjunction (and, but, so) joins two independent clauses with just a comma before it; a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover) needs a semicolon before it and a comma after, and can also open a new sentence.
cards.n: Using a comma alone before however creates a comma splice - a mechanical error MC revision questions test directly.

cards.q: Contrast cohesion and coherence in writing.
cards.a: Cohesion is the local, sentence-to-sentence stitching, such as pronouns, repeated terms, and transitions; coherence is the larger sense that the whole piece makes sense and moves toward a purpose.
cards.n: Writing can be cohesive at the sentence level while still failing to cohere as an argument.

cards.q: Identify what breaks a line of reasoning even when each paragraph is individually well written.
cards.a: Paragraphs that could be reordered without changing the essay's meaning, subclaims that repeat rather than build on each other, and body paragraphs that never connect back to the same governing thesis.

cards.q: State the MLA in-text citation format for a source with two authors.
cards.a: Both last names joined by and, followed by the page number, with no comma before the page: (Ruiz and Chen 42). If named in a signal phrase, only the page number appears in parentheses.

cards.q: Contrast a subclaim and a topic sentence.
cards.a: A subclaim is the idea a paragraph exists to prove, an arguable point that supports the thesis; a topic sentence is the actual sentence that states that subclaim to the reader.

cards.q: Explain why quoting an entire long sentence from a source usually weakens Row B more than a short quotation would.
cards.a: A long quotation leaves less room for commentary and often includes material the writer never analyzes, so the paragraph reads as evidence with thin explanation; a short, precisely chosen quotation lets nearly every word be unpacked.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question asking the function of a sentence or paragraph.
cards.a: Read the sentence in its surrounding context and ask what job it does for the argument - introduces a counterargument, provides an example, signals a shift, draws a conclusion - then choose the option naming that job.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question asking the effect of a specific word or phrase.
cards.a: Identify the word's connotation and what it implies about the writer's attitude toward the subject, then match that implication to the answer choice, eliminating options that describe the word accurately but miss its effect.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question about the relationship between two paragraphs.
cards.a: Name the logical move in your own words first - does the second paragraph exemplify, complicate, extend, or refute the first - then pick the answer choice matching that relationship.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question that asks you to identify a shift.
cards.a: Scan for markers - but, yet, however, a change in verb tense, a new pronoun, a sudden short sentence - locate the exact line where the shift occurs, then choose the answer naming both what changes and its direction.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang writing/revision question that asks which choice best adds evidence.
cards.a: Check the stated goal in the stem first, then test each option against the paragraph's existing claim: eliminate any choice that is off-topic, repeats a point already made, or is evidence with no clear link to that claim.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang writing/revision question that asks which choice best combines two sentences.
cards.a: Look for the option that subordinates the less important idea into a dependent clause or modifier while keeping the more important idea in the independent clause, preserving the original meaning.

cards.q: Explain the AP Lang MC 'EXCEPT' or 'NOT' question format and how to work it.
cards.a: The stem asks for the one choice that does NOT fit a stated pattern, so three of the four choices will be true and one false; work through options normally, tracking which you have confirmed true, and select the one left unconfirmed.
cards.n: Misreading EXCEPT and picking the first true answer is one of the most common careless MC errors.

cards.q: Explain whether a strong Row A thesis guarantees any Row B points.
cards.a: No. The rows are scored independently: an essay can earn the thesis point with a clear, defensible claim and still score low on Row B if the body paragraphs lack specific evidence or sustained commentary tied to a line of reasoning.
cards.n: Students sometimes over-invest in a polished thesis and under-invest in the body, where four of six points live.

cards.q: Contrast qualifying a claim and hedging (fence-sitting) on the AP Lang argument essay.
cards.a: Qualifying names specific conditions under which a position holds, committing to a precise, defensible claim; hedging avoids commitment altogether by presenting both sides as equally valid with no stance taken, which fails Row A.

cards.q: Explain whether a longer essay automatically scores higher on the AP Lang rubric.
cards.a: No. The rubric rewards specific evidence, sustained commentary, and a coherent line of reasoning, not word count; a shorter, tightly developed essay outscores a longer one padded with summary or repetition.

cards.q: Explain a fast brainstorming technique for choosing Q3 argument evidence under time pressure.
cards.a: Scan two mental buckets - lived or observed experience, and public knowledge such as history, current events, or reading - and grab the first specific, nameable example from each; a concrete detail beats a vague claim you cannot support.

cards.q: Explain the expected length and development of an AP Lang FRQ response.
cards.a: There is no minimum word count or page requirement; readers score the quality of the thesis, evidence, and commentary, not length. Fully developed essays with a real line of reasoning tend to run long, but padding does not help.

cards.q: Explain what the context note before each Section I passage typically provides.
cards.a: A brief framing statement giving the source, author, approximate date, and situation - enough of the rhetorical situation to identify audience and occasion without reading the full passage first.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a Q2 passage whose intended audience shifts partway through.
cards.a: Treat the shift itself as a rhetorical choice worth analyzing: identify where the address changes, such as from the general public to policymakers directly, and explain what that pivot allows that a single audience would not.

cards.q: Explain how to handle an AP Lang argument prompt built on a metaphorical or figurative quotation.
cards.a: Translate the figurative language into a literal, arguable claim before drafting a thesis - state in plain terms what the metaphor asserts about human behavior or society - so your argument responds to that claim.
cards.n: Essays that never unpack the metaphor tend to drift into paraphrase instead of argument.

cards.q: Explain whether AP Lang FRQs must be written in the printed order.
cards.a: No. You may write the three essays in any order within the 2 hour 15 minute block; the 15-minute period is designated reading time for the Q1 sources, but a student stronger elsewhere may start with Q2 or Q3 instead.

cards.q: Explain how to use line references in AP Lang MC question stems efficiently.
cards.a: Locate the cited line numbers in the margin, then read a few lines before and after rather than the single line alone, since the correct answer usually depends on context the isolated line does not supply.

cards.q: Explain a triage plan for Q1 or Q2 when time is running out mid-essay.
cards.a: Stop drafting new paragraphs and write a clear final sentence for the paragraph in progress, then use remaining minutes for one concise concluding statement that names the stakes, rather than starting a point you cannot finish.
cards.n: An unfinished paragraph with no landing sentence reads as more disorganized than a shorter, complete essay.

cards.q: Explain the benefit of preparing a flexible thesis template before exam day.
cards.a: A reusable frame, such as naming a position, listing supporting grounds, and acknowledging a limit, lets you draft a defensible, roadmap thesis quickly under time pressure without inventing sentence structure for each new prompt.

cards.q: Explain the AP Lang rubric's holistic scoring principle within Row B.
cards.a: Readers weigh the essay's evidence and commentary as a whole rather than checking off a fixed list of required moves; two essays with different structures can both reach a 4 if each sustains specific evidence and consistent explanation.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question about a chart, graph, or image embedded in a passage.
cards.a: Read the title, axis labels, or caption first to establish what is being measured, then treat the visual as an argument with its own claim, asking what choice in its design shapes how a viewer reads it.

cards.q: Explain the risk of overquoting a Q2 passage instead of quoting selectively.
cards.a: Copying long stretches of the passage leaves little room to explain any of it, so the paragraph reads as evidence with thin commentary; a few precise words analyzed closely earn more Row B credit than a long, under-analyzed quotation.

cards.q: Explain how AP readers are trained to stay consistent across thousands of essays (norming).
cards.a: Before scoring, readers practice on sample essays already scored by table leaders, discussing borderline cases until their judgments align, which is why the same rubric language produces consistent scores across many readers.

cards.q: Explain how to choose a position on an AP Lang argument prompt when you have no strong personal opinion.
cards.a: Pick the side you can support with the most specific, concrete evidence, not necessarily the side you believe most strongly - the rubric rewards a well-argued defensible position, not sincerity.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The senator, a decorated veteran, refused to discuss the vote.'
cards.a: An appositive: 'a decorated veteran' renames senator, adding a credential in a compact aside rather than a full clause.
cards.n: Appositives let a writer smuggle in characterization or credibility without slowing the sentence with a new clause.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The crowd fell silent, its collective breath held, as the verdict was read.'
cards.a: An absolute phrase: 'its collective breath held' modifies the whole main clause rather than a single noun, adding a vivid simultaneous detail.
cards.h: → noun + participle modifying the whole clause
cards.n: Absolute phrases modify the whole clause, not a single word, which is why they resist being folded into a simple adjective.

cards.q: Explain why a writer would set an appositive off with dashes instead of commas.
cards.a: Dashes make the appositive feel like an interruption or emphasis, drawing the reader's eye, while commas fold it in more quietly as background information.
cards.n: The grammar is identical either way; the punctuation choice is entirely about how much attention the aside should get.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of stacking two absolute phrases in one sentence.
cards.a: Stacked absolute phrases let a writer layer several simultaneous images or conditions onto one main action, creating a cinematic, slow-motion effect.
cards.n: Overusing this move across many sentences can feel overwritten, so save it for a single high-impact moment.

cards.q: Apply subordination to this pair to emphasize the job loss: 'The town lost its factory. Three hundred jobs disappeared overnight.'
cards.a: Subordinate the first idea: 'When the town lost its factory, three hundred jobs disappeared overnight,' putting the emphasis in the independent clause on the jobs.
cards.n: Whatever sits in the independent clause reads as the sentence's main point; the subordinate clause supplies background.

cards.q: Apply coordination to this pair to give both ideas equal weight: 'The mayor cut the ribbon. Protesters lined the sidewalk.'
cards.a: Coordinate them with a conjunction: 'The mayor cut the ribbon, and protesters lined the sidewalk,' which keeps both images equally prominent instead of subordinating either.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a semicolon, a colon, and a dash used at the same junction in a sentence.
cards.a: A semicolon balances two equal, related ideas; a colon announces that an explanation or list is about to deliver on a promise; a dash breaks in for emphasis or an abrupt aside.
cards.n: Three punctuation marks can often connect the same two ideas, but each frames the reader's expectation differently.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The board had one option left: resign.'
cards.a: The colon sets up the single word 'resign' as a blunt, delayed payoff, giving it more weight than a comma would.
cards.n: A colon promises that what follows will deliver on what came before; here the promise is a one-word gut punch.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The vote was close; the consequences were not.'
cards.a: The semicolon signals that the two clauses are tightly related and worth weighing against each other, without subordinating either one.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The plan was approved - barely - after three hours of debate.'
cards.a: The dashes interrupt the sentence to insert 'barely' as a pointed aside, forcing the reader to notice how narrow the approval was.
cards.n: Dashes read as more informal and abrupt than parentheses, which cushion an aside more gently.

cards.q: Contrast anaphora and epistrophe by where the repeated words fall.
cards.a: Anaphora repeats words at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences, while epistrophe repeats them at the end; anaphora drives forward and epistrophe hammers a close.
cards.n: Some passages use both at once, repeating a word at a clause's start and again at its end, so trace the repetition physically through the sentence.
x: repetition at the start vs. the end

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we can not' at the start of each clause builds toward the admission that words cannot match the soldiers' sacrifice.
cards.n: Lincoln uses the anaphora to deflate the ceremony itself before redirecting attention to the unfinished work of the living.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Kennedy's inaugural: 'we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship.'
cards.a: Parallelism — a tricolon of three matched verb-plus-object phrases with 'any' in the same slot each time. It is NOT anaphora: the clauses begin with pay, bear and meet, and anaphora needs the repeated word at the start of each clause.
cards.h: → name the scheme, and say why it is not anaphora
cards.n: A standing trap: repetition in the same position inside each clause is still not anaphora unless that position is the beginning.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people.'
cards.a: A tricolon on parallel prepositional phrases, with 'the people' repeated at the end of each - closer to epistrophe than anaphora since the repetition lands at the close.
cards.n: This line is often mislabeled as anaphora; the repeated words fall at the end of each phrase, not the start.

cards.q: Identify the device in Kennedy's inaugural: 'Ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: Antithesis and antimetabole - antimetabole being the chiasmus in which the identical words come back reversed: country/you, then you/country, sharpening the contrast between receiving and giving.
cards.n: Naming antimetabole rather than the broader chiasmus shows a reader you can see the exact structure, not just the contrast.

cards.q: Contrast the two devices at work in Kennedy's line 'ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: It is antithesis because it opposes two contrasting ideas, and chiasmus because the second clause reverses the grammatical order of the first.
cards.n: A single line can carry more than one device at once; identify both the contrast and the mirrored structure.

cards.q: Identify the technique Swift leans on in A Modest Proposal by having an economist calmly recommend eating Irish infants.
cards.a: A sustained ironic persona whose deadpan logic exposes the real cruelty of English policy toward the Irish poor, rather than stating the criticism directly.

cards.q: Identify the satire type in A Modest Proposal.
cards.a: Juvenalian satire; Swift's proposal is bitter and biting, using shocking irony to condemn real suffering rather than to gently amuse.
cards.n: Because the target is real, ongoing suffering rather than a mild social habit, calling this Horatian would badly undersell the essay's anger.

cards.q: Explain why A Modest Proposal's title is itself ironic.
cards.a: Calling a proposal to eat infants 'modest' signals from the first word that the speaker's calm reasonableness cannot be trusted, priming readers to look past the surface argument.

cards.q: Identify the rhetorical move King uses throughout Letter from Birmingham Jail before answering each clergyman's objection.
cards.a: Concession: he restates each objection fairly and sympathetically before refuting it, which makes the refutation harder to dismiss as unfair.
cards.n: This concession-then-refute pattern runs through nearly every section of the letter, not just one paragraph.

cards.q: Identify the primary appeal King builds by opening Letter from Birmingham Jail with his credentials and pastoral role.
cards.a: Ethos; establishing himself as a reasonable, credentialed clergyman answering fellow clergymen makes his later, more urgent claims harder to dismiss as extremism.

cards.q: Explain how King's long catalog sentence about lynchings and daily humiliations builds pathos in Letter from Birmingham Jail.
cards.a: Piling clause after clause of lived detail overwhelms the reader with specifics, making the word 'wait' feel like an unbearable demand rather than a reasonable request.
cards.n: Name the effect on the reader, not just the pile-up of clauses, to earn credit for analysis rather than description.

cards.q: Identify King's stated audience in Letter from Birmingham Jail based on its opening line, and note who else was really listening.
cards.a: The eight white clergymen who had criticized his methods in print, though King wrote knowing the letter would reach a much wider public.
cards.h: → clergymen, with the public listening in
cards.n: Writing for a stated audience while expecting a wider one is itself a rhetorical strategy worth naming in an essay.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of Lincoln opening with 'Four score and seven years ago' rather than 'eighty-seven years ago.'
cards.a: The formal, almost biblical phrasing elevates the occasion to solemn historic weight from the first line, setting a dedication's tone rather than a report's.

cards.q: Define parody and give an example.
cards.a: A work that imitates another text's style or conventions closely enough to be recognized, exaggerating it for comic or critical effect.
cards.n: Parody depends on the audience recognizing the original; without that recognition the joke does not land.

cards.q: Define lampoon and give an example.
cards.a: A short, sharply mocking piece aimed at a specific person or institution, using ridicule rather than balanced argument to attack its target.
x: a piece that ridicules a specific target

cards.q: Define caricature and give an example.
cards.a: A description or portrayal that exaggerates a subject's distinctive features or traits to make them ridiculous, often reducing a person to one exaggerated trait.
cards.n: Caricature works because the exaggerated trait is still recognizably drawn from something real about the subject.
x: exaggerated portrayal of a real subject

cards.q: Contrast parody and lampoon by what each one imitates.
cards.a: Parody imitates a text's style or form to mock it, while lampoon attacks a specific person or institution directly without needing to imitate anything.
cards.h: → imitates a form vs. attacks a target
cards.n: A single piece can do both at once: parody a genre while also lampooning a specific person writing within it.

cards.q: Contrast caricature and stereotype as satirical tools.
cards.a: Caricature exaggerates a specific, real subject's own traits for comic effect, while a stereotype flattens an entire group into a generic, assumed set of traits.
cards.n: Caricature is a deliberate technique writers can be praised for; calling writing stereotyped is usually a criticism, not a technique.

cards.q: Decide which satirical tool fits: a cartoon exaggerates a senator's already-large ears and nose to mock his vote.
cards.a: Caricature; the humor comes from exaggerating the senator's own physical features rather than imitating a text or attacking an institution generally.

cards.q: Explain why a writer often subordinates the less important of two ideas rather than presenting them as separate sentences.
cards.a: Subordinating one idea signals to the reader which point is secondary, so the sentence argues for a hierarchy of importance instead of listing facts as equals.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'Determined to finish before dark, the crew worked through the storm.'
cards.a: A participial phrase, 'Determined to finish before dark,' opening the sentence and front-loading the crew's motivation before naming their action.
cards.n: Don't confuse this with an absolute phrase; a participial phrase modifies the subject specifically, not the whole clause.

cards.q: Explain the effect of opening a sentence with a participial phrase rather than the subject.
cards.a: It delays the main subject and verb, forcing the reader to hold a condition or motive in mind before learning who acted, which can heighten suspense or foreground cause.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a single absolute phrase versus a full subordinate clause conveying the same idea.
cards.a: An absolute phrase feels compressed and image-like, almost cinematic, while a subordinate clause with 'because' or 'as' makes the same relationship feel more logically explicit.
cards.n: Both can convey simultaneity or cause, but the absolute phrase reads as more literary and less argumentative.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of each clause builds mounting resolve through accumulation.

cards.q: Contrast a wry tone and a sardonic tone.
cards.a: Wry suggests dry, understated amusement that stays gentle even while pointing out irony, while sardonic is openly bitter and scornfully mocking.
cards.n: Both notice irony, but only sardonic wants to wound; mistaking one for the other overstates or understates a writer's hostility.

cards.q: Contrast an earnest tone and a sentimental tone.
cards.a: Earnest conveys sincere, serious conviction without irony, while sentimental leans on exaggerated emotion, often past the point the evidence actually supports.
cards.n: Calling sincere writing 'sentimental' is usually a criticism; the word implies the emotion is overdone.

cards.q: Contrast a critical tone and a contemptuous tone.
cards.a: Critical evaluates a subject's flaws while still treating it as worth serious engagement, while contemptuous dismisses the subject as beneath respect entirely.
cards.n: A critical review can still recommend something despite its flaws; a contemptuous one cannot.

cards.q: Contrast a cynical tone and a skeptical tone.
cards.a: Skeptical withholds belief until evidence is shown, staying open to persuasion, while cynical assumes bad motives in advance and doubts sincerity is even possible.
