cards.n: A skeptical writer can be won over; a cynical one has already decided the answer.

cards.q: Contrast an indignant tone and an irate tone.
cards.a: Indignant expresses controlled moral outrage at something unjust, while irate is raw personal anger with less concern for justifying the emotion.

cards.q: Contrast a condescending tone and a patronizing tone.
cards.a: Condescending talks down to a reader as intellectually inferior, while patronizing adds a false show of kindness or generosity to that same superiority.
cards.n: Patronizing is condescension wearing a smile; look for exaggerated gentleness toward the reader as the tell.

cards.q: Contrast a mocking tone and a playful tone.
cards.a: Playful teases without any real edge, inviting the reader to laugh along, while mocking aims the humor at a target to belittle it.
cards.n: The line often comes down to power: mocking someone with less power reads harsher than mocking an equal.

cards.q: Contrast a solemn tone and a somber tone.
cards.a: Solemn suggests formal seriousness fitting a ceremony or occasion, while somber suggests a heavier, gloomier mood without that formal, ceremonial quality.

cards.q: Contrast an ambivalent tone and an apathetic tone.
cards.a: Ambivalent reflects genuine, conflicting feelings pulling in two directions, while apathetic reflects a simple absence of feeling or concern at all.
cards.h: → torn between two feelings vs. feeling nothing
cards.n: An ambivalent writer usually shows both sides of the conflict on the page; an apathetic one shows neither.

cards.q: Contrast a nostalgic tone and a wistful tone.
cards.a: Nostalgic centers on longing for a specific remembered past, while wistful is a softer, more general yearning that need not be tied to memory at all.
cards.n: Wistful can describe wanting something that never existed; nostalgic requires an actual past to look back on.

cards.q: Decide the more precise tone word: a columnist writes about a scandal with restrained, amused detachment rather than anger. Wry or indignant?
cards.a: Wry; the detachment and dry amusement rule out indignant, which requires visible moral outrage rather than calm irony.

cards.q: Decide the more precise tone word: an obituary praises a stranger's kindness so heavily that the praise starts to feel unearned. Earnest or sentimental?
cards.a: Sentimental; once the emotion outruns what the details actually support, the writing reads as overdone rather than simply sincere.
cards.n: The tell is proportion: emotion this large needs correspondingly specific, earned detail to avoid feeling manufactured.

cards.q: Decide the more precise tone word: a reviewer says a film 'aspires to depth it never once demonstrates,' dismissing it entirely. Critical or contemptuous?
cards.a: Contemptuous; the line does not just point out a flaw, it dismisses the film as unworthy of the aspiration in the first place.

cards.q: Decide the more precise tone word: a retiree describes missing coworkers she no longer sees, without idealizing the job itself. Nostalgic or wistful?
cards.a: Wistful; she is not romanticizing the past workplace, only expressing a gentle, general longing for the people, so 'wistful' fits more precisely.
cards.n: If she had praised the job itself as better than it was, that idealizing would push the tone back toward nostalgic.

cards.q: Contrast a defiant tone and a resigned tone toward the same setback.
cards.a: Defiant signals refusal to accept the outcome and a will to keep fighting it, while resigned signals acceptance that the outcome cannot be changed.
cards.h: → still fighting vs. accepting the outcome

cards.q: Contrast what the Toulmin model and classical arrangement are each used for.
cards.a: Classical arrangement structures an entire speech or essay into ordered parts, while the Toulmin model breaks down the logical structure of a single claim wherever it appears.
cards.n: Students sometimes treat Toulmin as a rival organizational scheme for an essay, but it was designed to test logic, not replace an outline.
x: structuring a speech vs. testing one claim's logic

cards.q: Explain when a writer would use Toulmin analysis rather than classical arrangement while planning an argument essay.
cards.a: Toulmin analysis helps a writer test whether one claim's reasoning actually holds up before writing, while classical arrangement helps organize the finished sequence of the whole essay.

cards.q: Decide which argument structure fits: a writer wants to find common ground with a skeptical audience before proposing any solution.
cards.a: Rogerian argument; it opens by acknowledging the opposing view's validity, which classical arrangement's confrontational structure is not built to do first.

cards.q: Define hedging language and give an example.
cards.a: Wording that softens a claim to avoid full commitment, such as 'it could be argued' or 'some might say,' often used to dodge rather than sharpen a position.
cards.n: Hedging is not the same as being appropriately cautious; the problem is vagueness, not caution itself.

cards.q: Contrast a qualifier that strengthens an argument and hedging language that weakens one.
cards.a: A precise qualifier narrows exactly when and where a claim holds, showing control, while hedging language avoids commitment altogether, leaving the reader unsure what the writer believes.
cards.n: 'Under most circumstances' qualifies; 'it could maybe be said' hedges - the difference is whether the limit is specific.

cards.q: Identify the problem: 'Some people might think that social media could possibly be somewhat harmful in certain cases.'
cards.a: Excessive hedging; stacking 'might,' 'could possibly,' and 'somewhat' buries any actual claim under vague qualification.

cards.q: Explain where a concession is most effective when placed within a body paragraph.
cards.a: Early in the paragraph, before the writer's own point, so the refutation that follows gets the final, more memorable word.
cards.n: Placing the concession first also signals fairness to the reader before the writer starts pushing back.

cards.q: Explain the risk of placing a concession at the very end of an argument essay.
cards.a: Ending on the opposing view without refuting it can leave the reader's last impression favoring the counterargument instead of the writer's own thesis.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier to strengthen this claim: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students.'
cards.a: Add a scope qualifier: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students when access to test preparation is unequal,' narrowing the claim to what evidence can support.
cards.n: A vague qualifier like 'sometimes' would do less work than naming the actual condition, unequal access to test prep.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'Every bridge inspected this year showed rust damage, so the county's bridges are likely deteriorating faster than reports admit.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning; a general conclusion is drawn from a pattern in specific observed cases, so it is probable rather than certain.
cards.n: The word 'likely' in the conclusion is itself a clue that the reasoning is inductive rather than certain.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'All published city audits must be reviewed by the comptroller. This audit was published. Therefore this audit must be reviewed by the comptroller.'
cards.a: Deductive reasoning; the conclusion follows necessarily from the two premises, in the form of a syllogism.
cards.n: The modal has to carry through. Concluding 'therefore the comptroller reviewed it' would not follow - a rule that something must happen is not evidence that it did.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'Three of the last four mayors raised taxes in their first year, so the new mayor probably will too.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning; the prediction is drawn from a pattern of past cases, so it is likely but not guaranteed.

cards.q: Explain why an inductive argument can be strong even though its conclusion is never certain.
cards.a: Strength in inductive reasoning comes from the size and representativeness of the sample, not from logical necessity; better evidence makes the conclusion more probable, not proven.
cards.n: A single well-chosen counterexample can still weaken even a large inductive sample, which is why induction stays probabilistic.

cards.q: Apply deductive reasoning to reach a conclusion: 'All municipal water systems must test for lead annually. Elm Creek runs a municipal water system.'
cards.a: Therefore Elm Creek must test its water for lead annually - the conclusion follows necessarily once both premises are accepted.

cards.q: Identify the classical canon most at work when a writer chooses which of five strong points to actually include in a tight time limit.
cards.a: Invention; deciding what material belongs in the argument at all happens in invention, before arrangement or style come into play.
cards.n: Invention happens before a word of the essay is drafted, which is why timed planning belongs to this canon.

cards.q: Explain why pairing a statistic with a brief anecdote often persuades better than either alone.
cards.a: The statistic supplies scope and credibility while the anecdote supplies a human stake, so the pairing satisfies both a skeptical reader's logos and an engaged reader's pathos.

cards.q: Decide whether this is a defensible claim or an unqualified overclaim: 'Homework should never be assigned on weekends.'
cards.a: An unqualified overclaim; 'never' forecloses any exception a reasonable opponent could raise, making the claim easy to defeat with a single counterexample.
cards.n: Swapping 'never' for 'rarely,' or naming a specific condition, would make the same claim far harder to attack.

cards.q: Contrast how concession is used in Rogerian argument versus in classical refutation.
cards.a: Rogerian argument opens with a genuine concession to build trust before any claim is made, while classical refutation raises the opposing view only after the writer's own case, mainly to dismantle it.
cards.n: The order matters more than the content: the same concession lands very differently depending on where it sits.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This new bridge inspection policy must be flawed, since it was proposed by a councilman who once missed a budget deadline.'
cards.a: Ad hominem; the policy is dismissed by attacking the proposer's past record instead of addressing the policy's actual merits.
cards.h: → attacks the proposer, not the policy
cards.n: Notice the policy itself never gets addressed at all; that total silence on the merits is the fallacy's signature.

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best supports a claim about a long-term historical trend, and explain why.
cards.a: Historical example; a documented pattern across past cases shows the trend is not a one-time coincidence, which a single statistic or anecdote cannot demonstrate alone.

cards.q: Define what counts as a visual or quantitative source in an AP Lang synthesis set.
cards.a: Any source presented as a chart, graph, table, photograph, cartoon, map, or infographic rather than continuous prose, still counted as one of the required sources if cited.
cards.n: Students sometimes forget to cite these sources at all, treating them as decoration rather than as a required source.

cards.q: Explain the difference between describing a chart and analyzing one in a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Describing restates what the numbers or image show; analyzing explains why that trend or image matters to the writer's argument and what conclusion it supports.
cards.h: → what it shows vs. why it matters
cards.n: Row B rewards analysis; a sentence that only restates the chart's data reads closer to summary.

cards.q: Identify the mistake: an essay paragraph spends four sentences listing every number on a bar graph before stating any claim about them.
cards.a: Data-dumping; reciting the chart's figures without connecting them to an argument reads as summary rather than analysis.

cards.q: Explain how to cite a graph or chart source with no named author in an AP Lang synthesis essay.
cards.a: Cite it by its source label, such as (Source C), matching whatever label the exam packet assigns the visual source.
cards.n: The same labeling convention applies to a photograph, cartoon, or map with no named creator.

cards.q: Explain what a political cartoon contributes to a synthesis source set that a prose source usually cannot.
cards.a: A cartoon compresses an argument into a single symbolic image, letting a writer analyze visual choices like exaggeration or juxtaposition as evidence of the cartoonist's stance.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier while citing a graph: rewrite 'The chart proves teen screen time causes anxiety' to match what a correlational graph can actually support.
cards.a: 'The chart suggests a correlation between teen screen time and anxiety' - a graph showing two trends rising together supports correlation, not proof of causation.
cards.n: Two trends rising together is genuinely useful evidence; the error is only in overstating what that relationship proves.

cards.q: Explain how to put a statistic from a graph source into conversation with a claim from a prose source in the same paragraph.
cards.a: State the prose source's claim, then show the graph's numbers either confirming or complicating it, so the two sources visibly respond to each other rather than sitting in separate paragraphs.

cards.q: Decide which detail from a bar graph is more useful as synthesis evidence: the exact value of one bar, or the overall trend across all the bars.
cards.a: The overall trend; a single bar's exact value rarely supports an argument on its own, while the trend across the whole graph shows a pattern the writer can build a claim around.
cards.h: → pattern over a single data point
cards.n: An exact value still has a place in a sentence, but it should serve the trend the writer is arguing, not stand alone.

cards.q: Explain why a synthesis essay should still explain a chart's axis labels or units in a sentence before analyzing it.
cards.a: A reader who has not seen the source needs enough orientation to follow the analysis; skipping this can make even a sharp observation about the data confusing.

cards.q: Identify what is missing: a paragraph analyzes a photograph's composition in detail but never states what claim the photograph is meant to support.
cards.a: A stated claim; strong analysis of a visual source still has to connect back to the writer's own argument, not float as observation alone.
cards.n: Detailed formal analysis of an image can look impressive while still earning little credit if it never connects to the thesis.

cards.q: Explain why over-relying on the one visual source in a synthesis set can weaken an essay's line of reasoning.
cards.a: A single image usually cannot carry a whole paragraph's argument, so leaning on it alone tends to produce description instead of the sustained reasoning readers reward.

cards.q: Contrast the kind of commentary a chart's numbers can support versus what a photograph's composition can support.
cards.a: A chart's numbers support claims about scale, trend, or comparison, while a photograph's composition supports claims about emphasis, framing, or emotional appeal.
cards.n: A single source can sometimes offer both kinds of evidence, so look for whichever the writer's specific claim actually needs.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a visual source that seems to contradict the claims in the prose sources.
cards.a: Use the contradiction directly: acknowledge the tension and explain what it reveals, since disagreement among sources is exactly the material a strong line of reasoning can analyze.
cards.h: → contradiction is material, not a problem

cards.q: Define an infographic and explain why it can be treated as a single source even though it combines text and images.
cards.a: A design that blends text, icons, and data visuals into one unified piece; it counts as one source because it presents one coordinated argument, not several separate ones.
cards.n: Treat every element in the infographic, text and image alike, as part of one argument when analyzing it.

cards.q: Explain the risk of quoting a caption under a photograph as if it were the photograph's own analysis.
cards.a: The caption is the source's framing of the image, not the writer's own analysis, so leaning on it without adding independent commentary can read as summary rather than argument.

cards.q: Explain why an AP Lang MC answer choice containing 'always' or 'never' is often wrong even when it sounds plausible.
cards.a: Absolute words claim something holds in every case, and passages rarely support a claim that strong, so readers should test extreme-language choices against the text before picking them.
cards.h: → absolute language rarely matches nuanced text
cards.n: This is a useful first filter, not an absolute rule; occasionally an extreme-language choice is correct, so still check it against the text.

cards.q: Define a half-right answer trap on the AP Lang multiple-choice section.
cards.a: A choice that correctly names a device or idea in the passage but pairs it with the wrong effect, location, or explanation, making it attractive but incorrect.
cards.n: These traps are common because eliminating an answer that's 'almost right' feels riskier than picking one that's 'somewhat right.'

cards.q: Explain how to catch a half-right answer trap before selecting it.
cards.a: Check every clause of the answer choice against the passage, not just the part that sounds familiar, since test-writers often build the trap into the second half of the sentence.
cards.n: A choice can be true for the first ten words and false for the last five; read the whole thing.

cards.q: Identify why an answer choice that is technically true about the passage can still be wrong on an AP Lang MC question.
cards.a: Because it does not answer the actual question being asked - it may be true but irrelevant to the specific function, effect, or relationship the stem asks about.

cards.q: Explain the trap in an overly narrow AP Lang MC answer choice.
cards.a: A choice can describe only one small detail from the passage instead of the broader function or effect the question actually asks about, making it too limited to be the best answer.
cards.n: A narrow choice can still be literally true about the passage, which is exactly what makes it tempting.

cards.q: Explain the trap in an overly broad AP Lang MC answer choice.
cards.a: A choice can make a sweeping claim about the whole passage's purpose when the question only asks about a single sentence or paragraph's specific function.

cards.q: Decide what to do when two AP Lang MC choices both seem partly supported by the passage.
cards.a: Reread the question stem itself and pick whichever choice answers exactly what was asked, since one choice usually addresses the stem precisely and the other only adjacently.
cards.h: → match the choice to the stem
cards.n: Resist re-skimming the whole passage first; the stem itself usually narrows the choice faster than a fresh read.

cards.q: Identify the trap when an AP Lang MC choice states close to the exact opposite of the passage's actual effect.
cards.a: An opposite-effect distractor; it often reuses accurate vocabulary from the passage but reverses the direction of the effect, so skimming can mistake familiarity for correctness.

cards.q: State a workable time split for planning versus writing a single 40-minute AP Lang FRQ.
cards.a: Roughly 5 to 8 minutes planning and annotating, with the remaining 32 to 35 minutes writing, leaving a couple of minutes to proofread if time allows.
cards.n: Longer, denser passages may justify a minute or two more planning time, borrowed from the writing minutes rather than added on top.

cards.q: Explain why spending too little time planning a Q3 argument essay tends to hurt the score more than it seems to save time.
cards.a: Without a planned line of reasoning, body paragraphs tend to drift or repeat the same point, which costs Row B points that planning would have protected.

cards.q: Explain a fast way to select which sources to use first when planning the Q1 synthesis essay under time pressure.
cards.a: Skim each source for one sentence that could serve as a claim or a strong quotation, then group sources that agree or disagree with each other, since paired sources plan faster.
cards.n: This grouping step also gives the essay's line of reasoning a built-in structure before a single sentence is drafted.

cards.q: Decide which three sources to lead with when six are available and only 40 minutes remain: the two that agree, or two that clash plus one that complicates both.
cards.a: Two that clash plus one that complicates both; sources in tension give a line of reasoning more to analyze than sources that simply agree with each other.

cards.q: Decide the sophistication move: an essay's conclusion explains a specific real-world limit on when the thesis would not hold. Does this likely earn the point?
cards.a: Likely yes; naming a specific situation where the argument's logic breaks down shows genuine complexity, one of the recognized paths to the sophistication point.
cards.h: → names a real limit or exception
cards.n: This move works because it shows the writer understands the argument's boundaries, not just its strongest case.

cards.q: Decide the sophistication move: an essay repeats 'furthermore' and 'moreover' but never adds a new layer of reasoning. Does this earn the point?
cards.a: Likely no; transition words alone are not complexity, and readers are trained to look past vocabulary for genuine additional reasoning.

cards.q: Explain why explicitly writing 'this shows sophistication' in an essay does not earn the sophistication point.
cards.a: The point rewards the reasoning actually demonstrated in the writing, not a label claiming credit for it; readers score what the analysis does, not what it announces about itself.
cards.n: The same principle applies to writing 'this is a strong counterargument'; naming a move is not the same as making it.

cards.q: Apply a sophistication move to strengthen this flat claim: 'Social media harms teenagers.' Add one qualifying layer.
cards.a: 'Social media harms teenagers most acutely when parental oversight and offline friendships are both weak,' which adds a specific condition instead of a blanket claim.

cards.q: Explain the risk of choosing evidence for a Q3 argument essay based only on which example is most dramatic.
cards.a: A dramatic example that does not actually match the claim's logic can weaken the line of reasoning even while it entertains, so relevance should outweigh drama when choosing evidence.
cards.n: A less dramatic but tightly relevant example almost always outscores a vivid one that only loosely fits the claim.

cards.q: Decide the stronger evidence for a claim about school start times: one friend's tired mornings, or a cited study comparing two districts' start times.
cards.a: The cited study; it offers a comparison across a real sample, while the anecdote is a single case that cannot rule out other explanations.

cards.q: Explain how a flexible thesis template can still earn the sophistication point rather than just the thesis point.
cards.a: A template that builds in a qualifying clause or an acknowledgment of complexity from the start gives the writer a head start on sophistication, as long as the content is not generic.
cards.n: A template only helps if the writer still fills it with the specific complexity of that prompt, not a phrase reused every time.

cards.q: Decide what to prioritize with 3 minutes left and one body paragraph unfinished: adding a new example, or writing a one-sentence link back to the thesis.
cards.a: The link back to the thesis; an unfinished paragraph that at least states its point and ties to the thesis reads as more complete than one left as a dangling example.

cards.q: Explain how to decide which of the three FRQs to write first when none feels obviously easiest.
cards.a: Start with the essay whose sources or prompt you understood fastest on the first read, since early momentum on a clear plan matters more than tackling essays in printed order.
cards.n: Writing the clearest essay first also builds momentum and confidence for the harder two that follow.

cards.q: Explain why a distractor that repeats a passage's exact vocabulary is not automatically the correct answer.
cards.a: Test-writers often lift real words from the passage into wrong choices precisely because familiar language feels safe, so the words must still match the question's actual claim.
cards.h: → familiar wording is not proof of correctness

cards.q: Decide whether this earns the Row A thesis point: 'Social media has both benefits and drawbacks for teenagers.'
cards.a: No; the statement lists two sides without taking a defensible position, so it reads as a topic restatement rather than a claim a reader could argue against.
cards.n: Adding one clause that commits to a side, even a qualified one, would likely fix this thesis without much rewriting.

cards.q: Decide whether this earns the Row A point: 'Because it erodes attention faster than it builds connection, social media harms teens more than it helps.'
cards.a: Yes; it takes a defensible position and previews the reasoning, attention versus connection, the essay will use to support it.

cards.q: Explain why writing out a full topic sentence during planning, rather than just a keyword, saves time later.
cards.a: A full topic sentence forces the line of reasoning to be decided during planning, so the writer is not improvising the paragraph's actual claim mid-draft.
cards.n: A one-word plan like 'ethos' still leaves the actual claim to be invented under pressure mid-paragraph.

cards.q: Explain the difference in what an AP Lang prompt asks for when it says 'evaluate the extent to which' versus a straightforward 'argue.'
cards.a: 'Evaluate the extent to which' expects the essay to weigh how much the claim holds true, inviting a qualified position, while a plain 'argue' prompt leaves the degree of agreement more open.

cards.q: Decide how to spend an extra 2 minutes found at the end of the reading period: rereading a source, or outlining the thesis.
cards.a: Outlining the thesis; a written thesis and rough plan protect against losing the line of reasoning once writing begins, which matters more than one more pass over a source.
cards.n: A plan that exists only in the writer's head is easy to lose once the pressure of drafting begins.

cards.q: Explain why process-of-elimination works better than searching for the 'obviously right' choice on tricky AP Lang MC questions.
cards.a: Eliminating choices that are clearly false, off-topic, or too extreme narrows the field even when no option feels perfect, which is common on inference-heavy questions.

cards.q: Explain why rereading only the topic sentence of each body paragraph is a fast way to check an essay's line of reasoning before time runs out.
cards.a: If the topic sentences alone tell a coherent story of the argument's progression, the line of reasoning likely holds; if they repeat each other, the essay is probably circling one point.
cards.n: This same check works even faster if the topic sentences were written out fully during planning rather than left as fragments.

cards.q: Explain why the context note before a Q2 or Q3 passage should shape your annotation before you start writing.
cards.a: It signals the speaker, occasion, and audience the readers already expect you to use, so annotating with that lens from the first read saves time re-reading for it later.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.' (Gettysburg Address)
cards.a: Antithesis; contrasting 'say' and 'did' sets empty words against enduring action, undercutting the speech's own occasion to redirect focus to the soldiers.

cards.q: Apply an appositive to add a credential to this sentence: 'The engineer warned that the bridge was unsafe.'
cards.a: 'The engineer, a thirty-year veteran of municipal inspections, warned that the bridge was unsafe' - the appositive adds authority without a separate clause.
cards.h: → noun phrase, not a new clause
cards.n: An appositive works here because 'a thirty-year veteran' is a noun phrase, not a full clause with its own verb.

cards.q: Decide the flaw: the passage's metaphor undercuts the speaker's optimism, but an answer choice claims it reflects the speaker's nostalgia instead.
cards.a: A half-right trap; the choice correctly spots the metaphor but assigns it the wrong effect, so it fails even though it names a real device in the passage.
cards.n: The passage detail has to be checked against both halves of the choice, not just the noun it names.

cards.q: Explain why quoting a graph's exact figure can strengthen a synthesis claim more than a rounded summary of it.
cards.a: An exact figure, like 'rose from 12 to 47 percent,' shows the scale of a change precisely, while a vague summary like 'increased a lot' gives a reader nothing concrete to weigh.
cards.n: Precision also signals to the reader that the writer engaged closely with the source rather than skimming it.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might choose Rogerian argument over classical arrangement when addressing a hostile audience.
cards.a: Rogerian argument's opening concession lowers a hostile audience's defenses before any claim is made, while classical arrangement's direct confirmatio can read as combative and shut the audience down early.
cards.n: A hostile audience that feels attacked from the first sentence rarely reads far enough to hear the strongest evidence.

cards.q: Define the choice-effect-purpose chain in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: A model for building analysis: name the specific rhetorical choice, explain its effect on the audience, then connect that effect to the writer's larger purpose. Stopping after the effect leaves the analysis floating with no argument.
cards.n: Most flat commentary stops after 'effect' and never ties back to purpose - that link is what a reader is scoring.

cards.q: Explain what distinguishes analysis from evaluation on the AP Lang rhetorical analysis question.
cards.a: Analysis explains how and why a writer's choices work on an audience to serve a purpose. Evaluation judges whether the writer succeeded or was right, which the prompt never asks for.
cards.h: → how it works vs whether it's right
cards.n: Praising or criticizing the writer's position earns nothing on Q2 - stay inside the text's effect on its audience.

cards.q: Identify the flaw: an essay states a speaker 'uses an anecdote, a rhetorical question, and parallelism' and then moves on.
cards.a: This is device-spotting, not analysis - it names techniques without explaining how any one of them functions on the audience or advances the writer's purpose.
cards.n: This is one of the most common Row B point-losers - a reader cannot credit analysis that never actually happened.

cards.q: Contrast a rhetorical analysis paragraph organized by device and one organized by the writer's argumentative move.
cards.a: Device-based organization walks through techniques one at a time with no throughline. Move-based organization groups whatever choices serve one stage of the writer's argument, producing a line of reasoning instead of a list.
cards.n: Move-based paragraphs read as analysis of an argument; device-based paragraphs read as a scavenger hunt.

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis thesis must name the writer's purpose, not just restate the topic.
cards.a: A thesis that only states the topic gives nothing to analyze. Naming the purpose gives the essay a claim to prove and gives every body paragraph a job.

cards.q: Decide the stronger commentary: 'This shows the senator is passionate,' or 'the short sentences quicken the pace to convey urgency.'
cards.a: The second is stronger: it names the choice, the effect, and the purpose it serves. The first is a vague label with no textual anchor and could describe almost any passage.
cards.n: Any commentary that could be copy-pasted onto a different passage is too generic to earn Row B credit.

cards.q: Define the invoked audience in rhetoric.
cards.a: The audience a text constructs or addresses within itself, through its assumptions, tone, and references, whether or not every actual reader matches that profile.
cards.n: A speech invoking 'my fellow citizens' invokes a national audience even if only a few hundred people are physically present.

cards.q: Contrast the invoked audience and the actual audience of a text.
cards.a: The invoked audience is who the text's language and assumptions address, such as concerned parents. The actual audience is whoever really reads or hears it, which may be far broader, including critics and historians.
cards.n: A published letter can invoke one small audience while its real audience is anyone who later reads it in print.

cards.q: Explain how a writer adapts diction for a specialist audience versus a general audience.
cards.a: For specialists, a writer can use technical terms without defining them and assume shared background knowledge. For a general audience, the writer defines jargon and slows the reasoning a specialist would skip.
cards.n: Overusing technical jargon with a general reader is as much a rhetorical misstep as underexplaining to an expert one.

cards.q: Define a captive audience and explain how it changes rhetorical strategy.
cards.a: An audience that must receive a message regardless of interest, such as students in a mandatory assembly. Because their attention is not already won, a writer must work harder to earn engagement rather than assume initial interest.
cards.h: → audience that must listen, whether interested or not
cards.n: A captive audience is not automatically a hostile one - it is simply not a self-selected one.

cards.q: Apply audience analysis: a price-hike memo will reach both loyal customers and industry regulators. What adjustment does this demand?
cards.a: The writer must address two audiences with different concerns in one text - reassuring customers with tone and value language while giving regulators the factual justification they need, without contradicting either.
cards.n: Writing to a mixed audience means no single appeal can dominate the whole text.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to justify.
cards.a: To provide reasons or evidence that make a past or proposed action appear reasonable, necessary, or fair, often used when the action is controversial or has drawn criticism.
cards.n: Justify differs from persuade: it defends a decision already made or about to be made, rather than winning a reader to a wholly new position.
x: give reasons an action was fair

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inspire.
cards.a: To move an audience toward hope, ambition, or renewed commitment by appealing to shared ideals rather than by presenting new evidence or arguing a contested claim.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to apologize (atone).
cards.a: To acknowledge wrongdoing, accept responsibility for it, and express genuine regret, typically to repair damaged trust rather than to argue a claim.
cards.n: A weak apology shifts blame or hedges responsibility; genuine atonement names the harm specifically.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to mobilize.
cards.a: To move an audience from agreement to action, giving them a specific, immediate step to take rather than simply changing what they believe.
cards.n: Mobilize goes further than persuade - the audience may already agree; the text asks them to act now.
x: move an audience to act now

cards.q: Decide the purpose: a CEO's memo after a data breach names exactly what happened, states who is responsible, and outlines concrete remedies.
cards.a: To justify combined with an implicit apology - the memo defends the company's response to a controversial event while accepting responsibility for the breach.
cards.n: Real texts often blend purposes; naming the dominant one and its secondary purpose is stronger than forcing a single label.

cards.q: Define arrangement as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing how a speaker organizes ideas into an effective structure, deciding the order in which claims, evidence, and appeals appear for maximum impact.
cards.n: This is the same organizational thinking behind classical arrangement, just named as one of the five canons.

cards.q: Define style as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing word choice, sentence structure, and figurative language, and how a speaker adapts these to purpose, audience, and occasion.
cards.n: This canon-level 'style' is the same concept the Style unit expands into devices, syntax, and tone.

cards.q: Define memory as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing a speaker's preparation to deliver a speech without total reliance on a written text, historically through memorization techniques, and now also internalizing an argument well enough to adapt it live.
cards.n: Memory is the canon AP Lang tests least directly, since the exam is written, not delivered aloud.

cards.q: Contrast the canon of invention and the canon of arrangement.
cards.a: Invention is the process of discovering what to say - generating arguments, evidence, and appeals. Arrangement is the separate process of deciding the order in which that already-discovered material should appear.

cards.q: State which classical canon governs a writer's decision to open with an emotional story rather than a statistic.
cards.a: Arrangement - the canon that governs the order and placement of material, including which piece of evidence leads.
cards.n: Invention would cover choosing the story and statistic in the first place; arrangement covers which comes first.

cards.q: Contrast a warrant and its backing in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: The warrant is the usually unstated assumption that connects the data to the claim. The backing is the further support offered if that warrant itself is challenged.
cards.h: → the assumption vs support for the assumption
cards.n: A warrant can be left implicit; backing is what you supply once someone asks why they should accept it.

cards.q: Identify the warrant: 'She graduated from a top engineering program, so she is qualified for the job.'
cards.a: The unstated assumption that graduating from a top engineering program indicates job qualification - that program prestige reliably predicts competence.
cards.n: Warrants are usually left unstated on purpose - saying one aloud that the audience does not share can backfire.

cards.q: Apply the Toulmin model: identify the data and claim in 'The reservoir dropped four feet, so the city should introduce watering restrictions.'
cards.a: Data (grounds): the reservoir dropped four feet this summer. Claim: the city should introduce watering restrictions.

cards.q: Explain why a rebuttal (reservation) makes a Toulmin argument stronger rather than weaker.
cards.a: Naming the specific conditions under which the claim would not hold shows the writer has tested the argument's limits, which makes the parts that do hold more credible, not less.
cards.n: This is the Toulmin-model version of a qualifier or concession elsewhere in argumentation.

cards.q: Define circumstantial evidence and give an example.
cards.a: Evidence that suggests a conclusion indirectly through surrounding facts rather than proving it directly, such as inferring a store was closed from its dark windows and empty parking lot rather than a posted sign.
cards.n: Circumstantial evidence can be persuasive in volume but is weaker than direct evidence alone.

cards.q: Define precedent as a form of evidence.
cards.a: A prior decision, event, or established practice cited to support how a current or future case should be treated, on the logic that like cases deserve like treatment.
cards.h: → prior case used to justify a new one
cards.n: Precedent is common in legal and policy arguments but weaker when the two cases differ in a way that matters.
x: a prior case used to justify a new one

cards.q: Contrast quantitative and qualitative evidence.
cards.a: Quantitative evidence is numerical - statistics, measurements, survey percentages. Qualitative evidence is descriptive - interviews, observations, case studies - capturing nuance numbers alone can miss.
cards.n: A strong Q1 synthesis essay often pairs one quantitative source with one qualitative source rather than relying on only one kind.

cards.q: Define a case study as a form of evidence and note its main limitation.
cards.a: An in-depth examination of one instance, person, or event used to illustrate a broader claim. Its limitation is that a single case may not generalize to the wider population.

cards.q: Decide the stronger evidence for a claim that a new policy is effective nationwide: one detailed case study, or a smaller statistic drawn from many locations.
cards.a: The multi-location statistic, because it demonstrates the effect holds across contexts. A single case study is vivid but cannot show the pattern generalizes.
cards.n: Vividness and representativeness are different strengths - a case study wins the first, a broad statistic wins the second.

cards.q: Define a claim of cause and give an example.
cards.a: A claim asserting that one thing brings about another, such as 'Reduced recess time has caused a rise in childhood anxiety.' It requires evidence of a causal link, not just a correlation.
cards.n: Claims of cause are the easiest claim type to overreach on - correlation is not causation.

cards.q: Define a claim of definition and give an example.
cards.a: A claim asserting how a term or category should be understood, such as 'Vaping counts as tobacco use under the school's policy.' The argument turns on establishing criteria for the category.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'The plant closure caused unemployment to double in the county within a year.'
cards.a: A claim of cause - it asserts that one event directly produced another, which requires evidence ruling out other explanations.
cards.n: Watch for claims of cause disguised as claims of fact - a causal verb like 'caused' is the giveaway.

cards.q: Explain why a claim of cause needs stronger evidence than a claim of value to be defensible.
cards.a: A claim of cause must rule out coincidence and other explanations to show one thing actually produced another, while a claim of value only needs to justify a judgment against stated criteria, a lower evidentiary bar.
cards.h: → ruling out alternatives vs justifying a judgment

cards.q: Define a necessary condition and a sufficient condition, and give an example distinguishing them.
cards.a: A necessary condition must be true for an outcome to occur, though it may not guarantee it; a sufficient condition guarantees the outcome on its own. Being 16 is necessary for a driver's license in most states but not sufficient, since passing the test is also required.
cards.h: → must happen vs guarantees it happens
cards.n: Confusing the two is a common source of invalid syllogisms on the exam.

cards.q: Explain the logical error of affirming the consequent in a conditional argument.
cards.a: Given 'if A then B,' affirming the consequent wrongly concludes A from the mere fact that B is true, ignoring that B could have other causes. Wet grass does not prove it rained, since a sprinkler could explain it too.
cards.h: → B being true doesn't prove A

cards.q: Identify the classical arrangement part: an essay's final paragraph issues a call to action and leaves a resonant final image.
cards.a: The peroratio - the concluding part of classical arrangement that sums up the argument and makes a final emotional appeal to move the audience to action.
cards.n: The peroratio is often where a writer risks overreaching with pathos after a carefully reasoned confirmatio.

cards.q: Contrast the narratio and the confirmatio in classical arrangement.
cards.a: The narratio lays out the background facts a reader needs to understand the dispute; the confirmatio presents the actual arguments and evidence supporting the writer's claim.
cards.h: → background facts vs the actual case
cards.n: Students often skip a narratio, but a reader who lacks context cannot fairly judge the confirmatio that follows.

cards.q: Explain why opening an AP Lang essay with a broad, generic claim about 'society' or 'history' usually hurts more than it helps.
cards.a: A generic opening delays the actual argument, wastes limited time, and often produces an unfalsifiable statement no one could disagree with, working against a specific, defensible thesis.
cards.h: → wastes time, produces an unfalsifiable claim

cards.q: Identify the introduction habit: an essay opens by defining a dictionary word from the prompt before making any claim.
cards.a: The dictionary-definition opening - a low-value move that consumes a sentence without advancing an argument, since dictionary definitions rarely illuminate the actual dispute.
cards.n: A prompt's own key term rarely needs 'the dictionary defines X as' - readers already know common words.

cards.q: Contrast a hook that earns its place in an AP Lang introduction and one that only delays the thesis.
cards.a: A hook that earns its place connects directly to the essay's claim, such as a striking detail from the passage or sources. A hook that only delays the thesis is a generic anecdote with no clear link to the argument that follows.
cards.n: If you could delete the opening sentence and lose nothing, delete it.

cards.q: Apply an effective opening move: write a one-sentence introduction opener for an essay arguing that social media has weakened, not strengthened, local news.
cards.a: A strong opener states the stakes directly: as local newspapers close by the hundreds, the platforms that promised to replace them have instead hollowed out the audience that once kept them alive.

cards.q: Explain how an effective AP Lang conclusion differs from a simple restatement of the thesis.
cards.a: An effective conclusion extends the argument's implications, such as its stakes or a broader consequence, rather than repeating the same sentence in different words, which adds nothing a reader has not already read.

cards.q: Identify the conclusion habit: an essay's final paragraph introduces a brand-new piece of evidence not discussed anywhere in the body.
cards.a: A new-evidence conclusion - introducing unsupported material this late leaves no room to develop it and can read as an afterthought rather than a synthesis of the argument.
cards.h: → new evidence too late to develop
cards.n: Save new evidence for a body paragraph; the conclusion's job is to make the existing case land, not expand it.

cards.q: Contrast a conclusion that broadens the stakes of an argument and one that merely summarizes the body paragraphs.
cards.a: A conclusion that broadens the stakes connects the specific claim to a larger consequence, giving the argument weight beyond the essay itself. A summarizing conclusion just restates each point already made, adding no new value.
cards.n: Broadening the stakes is often where Row C sophistication is earned in a conclusion.

cards.q: Explain the risk of ending an AP Lang essay mid-argument because time ran out.
cards.a: An essay that stops without any concluding move loses the chance to reinforce the line of reasoning, though a reader typically will not penalize length alone if the thesis and evidence rows are already earned.
cards.n: A one-sentence wrap-up beats no conclusion at all, but never at the cost of an undeveloped body paragraph.

cards.q: Explain how topic sentences reveal whether an essay has a genuine line of reasoning.
cards.a: If the topic sentences of every body paragraph, read in sequence with nothing else, form a logical progression that builds toward the thesis, the essay has a line of reasoning; if they read as an unordered list, it does not.
cards.h: → read only the topic sentences in order

cards.q: Contrast a line of reasoning built on addition and one built on escalation.
cards.a: An additive line of reasoning stacks separate, roughly equal reasons side by side. An escalating line of reasoning orders reasons so each builds on or intensifies the one before it, ending on the strongest point.
cards.n: An escalating structure often reads as more sophisticated, since the order itself becomes part of the argument.

cards.q: Identify the problem: an essay's three body paragraphs each restate the thesis in different words instead of advancing a distinct reason.
cards.a: The paragraphs are redundant rather than progressive - a line of reasoning needs each paragraph to contribute a new, distinct reason, not repeat the same idea with different examples.
cards.n: Padding an essay with lightly reworded restatements is a common trap of five-paragraph autopilot.

cards.q: Explain why a line of reasoning matters more to an AP Lang score than the number of body paragraphs.
cards.a: Row B rewards a coherent line of reasoning across the essay, not a paragraph count; three tightly connected paragraphs that build an argument outscore five that repeat the same point in different words.

cards.q: Define a transitional echo as a coherence device.
cards.a: Restating a key word or idea from the end of one paragraph at the start of the next, so the connection between them is explicit rather than assumed.

cards.q: Explain how parallel sentence structure across paragraphs can build coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Repeating a grammatical pattern at each paragraph's opening or closing signals that the paragraphs are doing comparable work in the argument, helping a reader track the essay's structure without extra explanation.

cards.q: Identify the coherence problem: an essay uses 'this' five times in one paragraph, each time pointing to a different idea from the sentence before.
cards.a: Vague pronoun reference - 'this' with no clear single antecedent forces a reader to guess which idea it points to each time, breaking the paragraph's coherence.
cards.n: A quick fix is to add a noun right after 'this,' such as 'this pattern' or 'this omission,' so the reference is never ambiguous.

cards.q: Contrast global coherence and local coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Global coherence is whether the essay as a whole builds toward its thesis across paragraphs. Local coherence is whether sentences within a single paragraph connect smoothly to each other.
cards.n: A paragraph can read smoothly sentence to sentence and still fail to advance the essay's larger line of reasoning.

cards.q: Explain the risk of a body paragraph that opens with evidence instead of a topic sentence.
cards.a: Without a topic sentence framing the claim first, a reader must infer the paragraph's point from the evidence alone, which can obscure the argument even when the evidence itself is strong.
cards.n: A reader should never have to reverse-engineer a paragraph's claim from the quotation alone.

cards.q: Identify the problem: a body paragraph presents two unrelated pieces of evidence for two different subclaims without transitioning between them.
cards.a: The paragraph lacks unity - a single paragraph should develop one controlling idea; two subclaims crammed together without a transition should be split into two paragraphs or connected explicitly.

cards.q: Explain the evidence-to-commentary ratio a strong AP Lang body paragraph should aim for.
cards.a: Commentary explaining and connecting the evidence should outweigh the evidence itself, often two or three sentences of analysis for every one sentence of quoted or cited material.
cards.n: A paragraph that is mostly quotation with a one-sentence wrap-up rarely earns full Row B credit.

cards.q: Explain the concession-turn-refutation pattern for handling a counterargument in one sentence.
cards.a: State the opposing point honestly, mark a pivot with a word like 'however' or 'yet,' then explain why the writer's position still holds. Skipping the turn leaves the concession unanswered.

cards.q: Identify the turn word doing the work in: 'Critics are right that the program is costly. Yet the cost of inaction is far higher.'
cards.a: 'Yet' - it signals the pivot from conceding the critics' point to refuting it by reframing the comparison.
cards.n: Other common turn words include 'however,' 'but,' 'still,' and 'nonetheless.'

cards.q: Explain the risk of devoting too much space to a counterargument in a body paragraph.
cards.a: If the opposing view is developed in more detail and with more vivid evidence than the writer's own refutation, the paragraph can end up making the other side's case more persuasively than the writer's.
cards.n: A counterargument should be stated fairly, but never argued more fully than it is answered.

cards.q: Contrast dismissing a counterargument and substantively refuting one.
cards.a: Dismissing a counterargument rejects it without engaging its logic or evidence, often in a single flat sentence. Substantively refuting it engages the opposing reasoning directly and shows specifically where it falls short.
cards.n: A dismissed counterargument reads as evasive to a reader and rarely earns sophistication credit.

cards.q: Explain how engaging a strong counterargument, rather than a weak one, can earn the Row C sophistication point.
cards.a: Choosing the opposition's best point and still answering it shows the writer has tested the argument against real resistance, which is the kind of complexity readers reward. Refuting an easy, straw-man version does not.

cards.q: Explain why signaling an essay's organizational pattern early helps a reader follow the argument.
cards.a: Naming the pattern in the introduction or first topic sentence, such as moving from most to least urgent, lets a reader predict how the argument will unfold and notice each new paragraph's role in that plan.
cards.n: This is a small move but a real one for Row C, since it shows deliberate control over structure.

cards.q: Decide the better organizational pattern for an essay arguing a city's transit failures caused a specific 2019 accident: chronological, or order of importance.
cards.a: Chronological - readers need the sequence of failures in the order they occurred to see how one led to the next; order of importance would obscure the causal chain the essay is arguing for.

cards.q: Explain how a synthesis essay thesis should engage with the range of provided sources without simply agreeing with all of them.
cards.a: A strong synthesis thesis stakes out the writer's own defensible position on the issue, using the sources as evidence for that position, even when the position aligns more with some sources than others.

cards.q: Identify the weakness: a synthesis essay cites three sources but never explains how any two of them relate to each other.
cards.a: The sources are listed, not synthesized - true synthesis puts sources in conversation with each other and with the writer's claim, not just alongside each other.
cards.n: A simple fix: end the paragraph with one sentence naming exactly how the two sources agree, disagree, or complicate each other.

cards.q: Define a parenthetical citation used for a source identified only by letter in the AP Lang synthesis source set.
cards.a: A citation using the source's assigned letter, such as (Source C), rather than an author's name, since synthesis sources are typically labeled A through F or G on the exam.
cards.n: This is the AP Lang exam's own shorthand, distinct from standard MLA author citation.

cards.q: Explain why citing a source by letter alone, with no attributive tag, is weaker than naming what the source is.
cards.a: '(Source B)' tells a reader nothing about the source's credibility or type, while a tag like 'a 2021 CDC report (Source B) found' lets the reader weigh the evidence while reading, not just after checking a citation.
cards.n: This costs little extra time and directly strengthens the credibility of the evidence being cited.

cards.q: Contrast 'which' and 'that' in formal written English.
cards.a: 'That' introduces a restrictive clause essential to identifying the noun and takes no comma; 'which' introduces a nonrestrictive clause adding extra, removable information and is set off by a comma.
cards.h: → essential, no comma vs extra, comma
cards.n: Misusing 'which' for a restrictive clause is one of the most common style errors AP readers notice, even though it rarely triggers a Row B penalty alone.

cards.q: Define a comma splice and give an example.
cards.a: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma with no coordinating conjunction, such as 'The evidence was strong, the jury still hesitated.' It should be a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a conjunction.
cards.h: → two sentences glued by just a comma
x: two sentences joined by only a comma

cards.q: Define a dangling modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive phrase placed so it appears to modify the wrong word, often because the word it should modify is missing, as in 'Having finished the report, the printer jammed,' where the printer did not finish the report.
cards.h: → modifier with no clear noun to attach to
cards.n: Dangling modifiers are common in rushed timed writing when a sentence gets restructured mid-thought.

cards.q: Contrast 'who' and 'whom' in formal usage.
cards.a: 'Who' is a subject pronoun, used when the pronoun performs the action, as in 'who wrote the letter.' 'Whom' is an object pronoun, used when the pronoun receives the action, as in 'to whom it may concern.'
cards.n: A quick test: if 'he' fits, use 'who'; if 'him' fits, use 'whom.'

cards.q: Define a misplaced modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive word or phrase positioned too far from the word it modifies, creating an unintended meaning, as in 'She almost drove her kids to school every day,' which suggests she rarely finished the drive rather than that she nearly did it daily.
cards.h: → modifier too far from its target word
cards.n: Reading the sentence and asking what word sits right next to the modifier usually catches the error fast.

cards.q: Explain the parallel structure error in 'The policy will reduce costs, improving morale, and it protects jobs.'
cards.a: The three items in a series should share the same grammatical form; mixing a base verb, a gerund, and a full clause breaks the parallelism. A corrected version reads 'reduce costs, improve morale, and protect jobs.'
cards.h: → match the grammatical form across a series
cards.n: Broken parallelism is easy to miss in a timed essay because each clause sounds fine read alone.

cards.q: Contrast a restrictive and a nonrestrictive clause.
cards.a: A restrictive clause narrows down which specific thing is meant and cannot be removed without changing the sentence's meaning. A nonrestrictive clause adds extra detail that could be deleted without changing which thing is meant.
cards.n: This same essential-vs-extra distinction underlies the which/that rule tested elsewhere in this unit.

cards.q: Explain why subject-verb agreement errors increase when a long prepositional phrase sits between the subject and the verb.
cards.a: A writer's ear tracks the noun closest to the verb rather than the true subject, producing errors like 'The list of items are long,' where 'list,' not 'items,' is the actual subject requiring a singular verb.
cards.h: → nearest noun, not the true subject, misleads the ear

cards.q: Define malapropism and give an example.
cards.a: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, producing an unintentionally absurd meaning, as in saying someone is 'the pineapple of politeness' instead of 'pinnacle.'
cards.h: → wrong word, similar sound, absurd result
cards.n: A malapropism is an error within the world of the text; authors often put one in a character's mouth on purpose to reveal something about them.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'That lawyer is a real wolf in cheap clothing.'
cards.a: Malapropism - 'cheap' is mistakenly substituted for the similar-sounding 'sheep's,' replacing the intended idiom with an absurd, unintended meaning.
cards.n: Malapropisms are a favorite device for characterizing a pompous or careless speaker in satire.

cards.q: Define bombast and give an example.
cards.a: Pompous, overblown language that is far more elevated or dramatic than its subject deserves, such as calling a minor scheduling conflict 'an unprecedented catastrophe.'
cards.h: → inflated language for a small subject

cards.q: Define vitriol and give an example.
cards.a: Harsh, bitterly critical language meant to wound or condemn, sharper and more personal in its hostility than ordinary criticism, such as branding an opponent's plan 'a con dressed up as compassion.'
cards.n: Vitriol and invective overlap; vitriol emphasizes bitterness, invective emphasizes direct verbal abuse.

cards.q: Define a vignette as a form of evidence in a passage.
cards.a: A brief, vivid scene or descriptive sketch used to illustrate a point through a single concentrated image rather than a fully developed narrative.
cards.h: → short vivid scene, not a full story
cards.n: A vignette differs from an anecdote in scale: an anecdote usually has a beginning, middle, and end; a vignette is closer to one frozen image.

cards.q: Contrast an anecdote and a vignette as forms of evidence.
cards.a: An anecdote is a brief story with a sequence of events leading to a point. A vignette is a single vivid scene or image with little to no narrative sequence, favoring atmosphere over plot.

cards.q: Define idiolect in style analysis.
cards.a: The distinctive, individual pattern of word choice, syntax, and speech habits unique to one speaker or writer, as opposed to the shared conventions of a whole dialect or era.
cards.h: → one writer's own signature pattern of language
cards.n: Analyzing a passage's idiolect matters most when a writer's individual voice, not any single device, is what drives the passage's effect.

cards.q: Explain how a sudden shift in register can function as a rhetorical choice within a passage.
cards.a: Dropping from formal, elevated diction into a blunt colloquial phrase, or the reverse, can jolt a reader's attention, signal sincerity breaking through formality, or mark a pivot in the writer's argument.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The White House issued a statement denying the allegations.'
cards.a: Metonymy - 'the White House' substitutes for the president or presidential administration, a closely associated entity standing in for what it represents.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'All hands were needed on deck before the storm hit.'
cards.a: Synecdoche - 'hands' stands in for the sailors as whole people, a part representing the whole.
cards.n: Synecdoche also runs the other way, whole for part: 'Germany beat Brazil' puts a nation in place of eleven players. Do not use 'Washington' for the government as the example — that is metonymy, an associated place standing in for an institution, like 'the White House'.

cards.q: Define a maxim and contrast it with an aphorism.
cards.a: A maxim is a short statement of practical wisdom meant as a guide to conduct, such as 'measure twice, cut once.' It differs from an aphorism mainly in emphasis: a maxim gives advice for action, while an aphorism states a general truth.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Fortune favors the bold.'
cards.a: An aphorism - a short, memorable statement expressing a general truth in a self-contained sentence.

cards.q: Explain why AP Lang essay scores from a student's three FRQs are summed rather than averaged before weighting.
cards.a: Each of the three essays earns its own 0-6 score independently against the rubric; these three scores are summed and then combined with the multiple-choice score according to the section weights to form the composite.

cards.q: Define an analytic (row-based) scoring model and contrast it with holistic scoring.
cards.a: Analytic scoring awards points row by row against fixed, named criteria, as the AP Lang essay rubric does. Holistic scoring assigns one overall impression score without breaking the judgment into separate criteria.
cards.h: → row-by-row criteria vs one overall impression
cards.n: Even though the overall rubric is analytic, Row B itself is scored holistically within its own 0-4 scale.

cards.q: Explain why an essay that only partly addresses a multi-part AP Lang prompt can still score well.
cards.a: Row A and Row B credit is earned by what the response does well against the rubric criteria, so a response that fully addresses most of the prompt with strong evidence and commentary can still earn most available points.
cards.n: This does not apply if the ignored part is the entire task, such as never taking a position on an argument prompt.

cards.q: Contrast how length and how quality separately affect an AP Lang essay score.
cards.a: Length alone earns no credit; a short, well-developed essay can outscore a long, repetitive one. Quality, meaning specific evidence and analytical commentary, is what the rubric rewards.

cards.q: Define the attribution line before each AP Lang Section I passage.
cards.a: A brief note giving the passage's author, title, date, and original context, which orients the rhetorical situation before you read a single sentence of the passage itself.

cards.q: Explain why every passage on the AP Lang exam is nonfiction.
cards.a: The course tests rhetorical analysis of real arguments and information, not literary interpretation of fiction, so every reading and writing passage is drawn from nonfiction genres such as speeches, essays, and articles.
cards.n: This distinguishes AP Lang from AP Literature, which is built around fiction and poetry.

cards.q: State roughly how many passages Section I of the AP Lang exam is built around.
cards.a: About five passages, split between reading-focused sets analyzing a published nonfiction text and writing-focused sets asking you to revise a student draft.
cards.n: The exact number can vary slightly by form, so treat five as a planning estimate, not a fixed count.

cards.q: Explain what changes about your reading approach for a writing/revision passage compared to a reading passage in Section I.
cards.a: A writing passage is a student's draft, not a polished professional text, so you read it looking for what could be improved to meet a stated goal, rather than analyzing why an already-effective choice works.

cards.q: Explain what the standard Q2 instruction to 'analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes' is directing you to do with your evidence.
cards.a: It signals that your job is to select specific choices, such as diction, syntax, or structure, and explain how each one serves the writer's purpose, rather than paraphrasing the passage's content or judging its argument.

cards.q: Contrast an AP Lang argument prompt that provides a specific quotation to respond to and one that poses an open question.
cards.a: A quotation prompt requires you to take a position on that exact claim, using its own key terms in your thesis. An open-question prompt gives more latitude to define the issue yourself, but still needs one clear, defensible position.
cards.n: Either type still requires one clear, defensible position - the prompt style changes your entry point, not the requirement.

cards.q: Explain the mistake of treating an AP Lang argument prompt as an invitation to write a personal narrative.
cards.a: The prompt asks for a defensible claim developed with evidence and reasoning, not a story about your own experience for its own sake; personal experience may serve as one piece of evidence, but it cannot replace an argument.
cards.n: A personal anecdote can open a body paragraph, but the paragraph still needs a claim and commentary, not just narration.

cards.q: Define what an AP Lang prompt means by a writer's 'rhetorical choices.'
cards.a: The deliberate decisions a writer makes in language and structure, such as word choice, sentence length and type, organization, appeals, and evidence, selected to achieve a specific effect on a specific audience.
cards.h: → deliberate decisions in language and structure
cards.n: This phrase appears in nearly every Q2 prompt verbatim, so it is worth having a ready checklist of choice categories.

cards.q: Decide the flaw: a Q3 argument essay never states the prompt's key term, 'civic duty,' anywhere in the thesis.
cards.a: The thesis fails to engage the prompt's actual terms, risking a reader's judgment that the essay argues a related but different claim rather than the one the prompt asked.

cards.q: Contrast whose argument a Q2 rhetorical analysis thesis makes and whose argument a Q3 argument essay thesis makes.
cards.a: A Q2 thesis argues about the writer's purpose and choices in someone else's text. A Q3 thesis argues the student's own position on the prompt's issue, developed with the student's own evidence.
cards.h: → analyzing another writer's argument vs making your own

cards.q: Explain why a Q2 passage is always provided in full while a Q3 argument essay is given no source passage at all.
cards.a: Q2 tests the ability to analyze an existing text's rhetorical choices, which requires that text to be present. Q3 tests the ability to construct an original argument from the student's own knowledge, so no passage is supplied.
cards.n: This is also why Q3 evidence must come from the student's own knowledge rather than close reading of a text.

cards.q: Explain what kind of source material typically makes up the Q1 synthesis source set.
cards.a: A mix of about six or seven sources in varied formats, such as prose articles, an image or cartoon, and a chart or graph, representing a range of perspectives on one debatable issue.

cards.q: Decide which FRQ is being described: the response must incorporate at least three outside sources into an original argument.
cards.a: Q1, the synthesis question - it is the only FRQ that requires citing a minimum number of provided sources as support for a position.
cards.n: Q2 and Q3 never require a minimum source count, since neither is built around a provided source set.

cards.q: Explain why rereading the Q2 passage's attribution line before drafting a thesis can prevent a common scoring mistake.
cards.a: The attribution line often names the speaker, occasion, and audience; missing it can lead to a thesis that misidentifies the rhetorical situation, which weakens every claim about purpose built on top of it.

cards.q: Explain whether an essay with no thesis statement anywhere can still earn Row B evidence and commentary points.
cards.a: Yes - Row A and Row B are scored independently. An essay that develops a defensible line of reasoning with strong evidence and commentary can earn substantial Row B credit even without a clean, isolable thesis.
cards.n: Never skip attempting a thesis, but losing the Row A point alone does not cap the rest of the essay.

cards.q: Define what a 'defensible' thesis means for the Row A point.
cards.a: A thesis making a claim a reasonable reader could disagree with, supported by reasoning rather than an obvious fact, a personal preference, or a claim beyond what the prompt or passage can support.
cards.h: → a claim someone could reasonably contest
cards.n: A thesis can be debatable and still be wrong to argue if the passage or sources cannot actually support it.

cards.q: Identify the rubric row a body paragraph with rich evidence but generic, repetitive commentary would lose the most credit on.
cards.a: Row B - evidence alone does not earn full credit; the commentary explaining how that evidence supports the line of reasoning is what the row is actually weighted toward.

cards.q: Explain why the AP Lang rubric rewards a thesis that is 'defensible' rather than one that is 'correct.'
cards.a: The rubric does not judge whether the reader agrees with the position, only whether the position is arguable and supportable; a well-reasoned essay defending an unpopular claim can score as high as one defending a popular claim.
